title: Fix Kubernetes client deploy mode
description:
Fixes #3506.

_Note: I used Opus 5.5 to help diagnose and fix this issue, but confirmed the fix manually in an interactive session._

## Summary

`spark_connect(master = "k8s://...")` fails with `Gateway in localhost:8880 did not respond` when `spark-defaults.conf` sets `spark.submit.deployMode cluster`. Two further bugs hid the real error from the user. This PR fixes all three:

| # | Bug | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | No `--deploy-mode` / `--master` passed to spark-submit for `k8s://` masters | The gateway is submitted as a separate driver pod, so nothing listens on `localhost:8880` (root cause) |
| 2 | Gateway retry loop in `start_shell()` uses `withCallingHandlers()` | The first failure escapes the loop: no retries, and `abort_shell()` never prints the spark-submit log |
| 3 | `sparklyr.log.console` is only read from `config` | `options(sparklyr.log.console = TRUE)`, which the error message recommends, has no effect |

The **sparklyr** gateway itself works fine as a Kubernetes client-mode driver, in the same way as PySpark's py4j JVM. It only needs spark-submit to be told to use client mode.

## Details

### 1. Client mode for `k8s://` masters (root cause)

For non-YARN masters, **sparklyr** calls spark-submit without `--master` or `--deploy-mode`. It sets the master later, through `SparkConf$setMaster()` inside the gateway, which is too late to choose the deploy mode:

```
spark-submit --name sparklyr --class sparklyr.Shell .../sparklyr-3.5-2.12.jar 8880 64382
```

So spark-submit falls back to `spark-defaults.conf`. The image we tested (Spark 3.5.4-amzn-0 on EKS) contains:

```
spark.master                     k8s://https://kubernetes.default.svc:443
spark.submit.deployMode          cluster
```

spark-submit then tries to launch `sparklyr.Shell` as a driver pod and fails straight away with `SparkException: Must specify the driver container image`. Even if an image were set, the gateway would be listening in a different pod.

**Change:** in `shell_connection()`, next to the existing yarn-cluster block, `k8s://` masters now get `--deploy-mode client --master <master>`. Each flag is added only if the user hasn't set `sparklyr.shell.deploy-mode` or `sparklyr.shell.master`. `spark_config_kubernetes()` sets both explicitly (cluster mode with port forwarding), so it is unaffected. A new internal helper, `spark_master_is_kubernetes()`, sits alongside `spark_master_is_yarn_cluster()`.

**Behaviour change:** users with a `k8s://` master who rely on cluster mode coming from `spark-defaults.conf`, without `spark_config_kubernetes()`, now need to set `sparklyr.shell.deploy-mode = "cluster"`. Before this change, that set-up only worked with custom gateway address and port-forwarding settings.

_(Broader option, left out of this PR: default to client mode for every non-local master except yarn-cluster. This would also cover standalone and Mesos defaults files that say `cluster`, but it affects more users.)_

### 2. Gateway retry loop

```r
withCallingHandlers(
  { gatewayInfo <- spark_connect_gateway(...); break },
  error = function(e) {
    if (gateway_connect_attempts > 0) {
      Sys.sleep(...)
      gateway_connect_retry_interval_s <- ...   # local to the handler, no effect
    } else {
      abort_shell(...)                           # prints the spark-submit log
    }
  }
)
```

`withCallingHandlers()` runs the handler and then lets the error keep propagating. With the default `gateway_connect_attempts = 5`, the first error escapes `start_shell()` after a sleep. `abort_shell()` is never reached, so the user sees only the bare gateway error and never the `---- Output Log ----` section with the real spark-submit exception. The back-off update is also lost, because it assigns to a variable local to the handler.

**Change:** the loop now uses `tryCatch()`, keeps the last error, and calls `abort_shell()` when it gives up. The error message includes the spark-submit log.

On timing: each attempt already waits up to `sparklyr.connect.timeout` (default 60s) in `wait_connect_gateway()`. If every attempt were retried in full, a gateway that never starts would take about 5 × 60s to fail. Instead, the loop stops retrying once `sparklyr.connect.timeout` has passed since the first attempt. Quick failures, such as connection refused while the JVM is still binding, are retried with back-off. A gateway that never comes up fails after about one timeout, as it does today. This is not a hard limit, because one attempt can still run past the timeout during the gateway's port query.

### 3. `options(sparklyr.log.console = TRUE)`

`sparklyr_gateway_trouble_shooting_msg()` suggests `options(sparklyr.log.console = TRUE)`, but `start_shell()` read the setting with `spark_config_exists()`, which only looks in `config`.

**Change:** the setting is now read with `spark_config_value()`, which falls back to `options()`:

```r
console_log <- !identical(
  spark_config_value(config, "sparklyr.log.console", FALSE),
  FALSE
)
```

As before, any value other than `FALSE` turns console logging on, so config values such as a YAML `"true"` keep working. `spark_submit()` already reads this setting through `spark_config_value()`.

## Tests

All tests are unit tests with mocks. They don't need Spark.

- `test-connection.R`: `spark_master_is_kubernetes()` matches `k8s://` (any case) and rejects
  `local`, `yarn`, `spark://` and `NULL`.
- `test-connection_shell.R`:
  - A `k8s://` master adds `--deploy-mode client --master <master>`.
  - Explicit `sparklyr.shell.deploy-mode` / `sparklyr.shell.master` settings (as set by
    `spark_config_kubernetes()`) are left alone.
  - Non-k8s masters are unchanged.
  - `start_shell()` retries after one gateway failure and then carries on.
  - When the gateway never starts, the error contains the spark-submit log; the test plants it
    through `SPARKLYR_LOG_FILE`. All 5 attempts are made.
  - `options(sparklyr.log.console = TRUE)` sends spark-submit output to the console.

### Verified

- Spark 3.5.4-amzn-0 (Scala 2.12), OpenJDK 17, R 4.6.1, in a pod on EKS, with the `spark-defaults.conf` shown above.
- With this branch installed, a plain `spark_connect(master = "k8s://...", config = <spark.* client-mode settings>)` connects. The config doesn't set `sparklyr.shell.deploy-mode` or `sparklyr.shell.master`, and only `sparklyr.shell.driver-memory` is passed at submit time. The session ran **DBI** queries and a **dbplyr** aggregation over a large Glue-catalog table on Kubernetes executors.
- On unmodified **sparklyr** 1.9.6, setting `sparklyr.shell.deploy-mode = "client"` and `sparklyr.shell.master = master` by hand connects in the same way. Without them it fails with `Gateway in localhost:8880 did not respond`.
- On **sparklyr** 1.9.6, `options(sparklyr.log.console = TRUE)` prints nothing extra. `config = list(sparklyr.log.console = TRUE)` prints the `Must specify the driver container image` exception.

title: Unwrap Scala Seq wrappers returned as java.util.List on the Spark 4 backend
description:
On Spark 4 (Scala 2.13), `invoke()` returns a `java.util.List` that wraps a Scala `Seq` as a single object reference instead of an R list. The most visible cases are `JavaRDD.take()` and `JavaRDD.collect()`, but anything that hands back a `Seq` through `.asJava` behaves the same way. On the Spark 3 backend the same calls return an R list, because `java/spark-2.4.0/serializer.scala` has:

```scala
case s @ SeqWrapper(_) => s.toArray
```

That case did not make it into `java/spark-4.0.0/serializer.scala`. It cannot be ported as written: Scala 2.13 moved the wrappers to `scala.collection.convert.JavaCollectionWrappers`, made them plain classes rather than case classes, and keeps the whole object `private[collection]`, so they cannot be named from `sparklyr`'s package. This change recognises `SeqWrapper`, `MutableSeqWrapper` and `MutableBufferWrapper` by class name and calls `toArray` on them, which is exactly what the Spark 3 backend does for `SeqWrapper`. Plain `java.util.List` instances (an `ArrayList`, for example) are still returned as object references, as before on both backends.

Reproduction with Spark 4.0.0 and the jar currently on `main`:

```r
jrdd <- sdf_len(sc, 3) %>% spark_dataframe() %>% invoke("javaRDD")
class(invoke(jrdd, "take", 2L))
#> [1] "spark_jobj" "shell_jobj"
```

With this change:

```r
str(invoke(jrdd, "take", 2L))
#> List of 2
#>  $ :List of 1
#>   ..$ : int 1
#>  $ :List of 1
#>   ..$ : int 2
```

Verification:

- Rebuilt `inst/java/sparklyr-master-2.13.jar` with `compile_package_jars()` against Spark 4.0.0 and scalac 2.13.15. Happy to drop the jar from the PR if you prefer to rebuild it yourself.
- Added a test to `test-core_invoke.R`. On Spark 4.0.0 it fails with the previous jar (6 of 7 expectations) and passes with the rebuilt one; `test-core_serialize.R` and `test-core_jobj.R` give identical results before and after.
- The Spark 3 backends are untouched.

Context: this surfaced while adding Spark 4 support to Apache Sedona's R package (apache/sedona#3338), which relies on `invoke()` returning R lists for `take()`/`collect()` results and needed a `toArray` workaround on Spark 4 (apache/sedona#3340).

description:

Adds a `urls` argument, so users can point to a different location if the files

title: Expands coverage testing, and applies fixes issues found throughout
description:
- Fixed `augment()` on a linear / generalized-linear-regression model when
`type.residuals` is not `"working"` (e.g. `"deviance"`, `"pearson"`,
`"response"`) and no `newdata` is supplied. It errored with "Can't rename
columns that don't exist" because `ml_predict()` drops the residuals column;
the residuals are now re-attached to the predictions.

- Fixed `names<-()` on a `tbl_spark` (e.g. `names(tbl) <- value`), which errored
with "Can't escape back tick from string" on recent `dbplyr`. The replacement
view is now re-registered using the bare remote table name instead of the
back tick-quoted `table_path`.

- Fixed `ml_gbt_classifier()` on Spark < 2.2 so a fitted classification model is
classed `ml_gbt_classification_model` (it was mislabeled
`ml_multilayer_perceptron_classification_model` due to a copy-paste error).

- Fixed `ft_robust_scaler()` so a fitted model is now wrapped as an
`ml_robust_scaler_model` object. `RobustScaler`/`RobustScalerModel` were missing
from the JVM-class mapping, so a fitted robust scaler fell back to a generic
`ml_transformer` (and the model constructor carried the estimator's class by
mistake). Transformation worked, but the model's class was inconsistent with the
other scalers.

- Fixed the `sparklyr.stream.collect.timeout` and
`sparklyr.stream.validate.timeout` configuration options being silently ignored.
The internal code referenced a bare `config` that resolved to an unrelated
imported function instead of the connection's configuration, so the timeouts
always fell back to their defaults; they now read from the active connection.

- Fixed `sdf_pivot()` so a multi-column pivot specification (the right-hand side
of the formula, e.g. `a ~ b + c`) is now correctly rejected with a clear
"pivot column is not length one" error. Previously the right-hand side was not
split on `+`/`*` (an errant `fixed = TRUE`), so such a formula failed later with
a confusing "missing variables in dataset" error instead.

- Fixed `spark_write()` and `spark_write_table()` when passed a `spark_jobj`:
the internal JVM class check only accepted `org.apache.spark.sql.DataFrame`,
which has not been the concrete class since Spark 2.0 (it is now
`org.apache.spark.sql.Dataset`, or `org.apache.spark.sql.classic.Dataset` on
Spark 4.x), so these methods always errored. The check is now version-agnostic.

title: ml_load(): use Spark SQL glob for metadata (supports UC /Volumes); keep legacy textFile fallback
description:
Problem
`ml_load()` fails to load models from Unity Catalog Volume paths (/Volumes/...) with IllegalArgumentException.

Root cause
`SparkContext.textFile(..., "metadata/part-00*")` path can be treated like local FS and trip UC access checks.
Spark SQL / DataFrameReader is UC-aware and resolves /Volumes correctly.

Change
- Prefer Spark JSON glob: `file.path(path, "metadata", "part-*")`, parse `class`, then `class.load(path)`.
- Keep the original textFile path as a fallback to avoid breaking edge cases.

Tests
- `tests/testthat/test-ml-load.R`: happy-path (glob) + forced-failure fallback.

No API changes; behavior is preserved on non-UC paths.

title: Support sparklyr connect for Azure Synapse Analytics
description:
# Description
This PR proposes to enable [Azure Synapse Analytics](https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/products/synapse-analytics) users to use `spark_connect(..., method="synapse")` to connect to an existing Azure Synapse Spark session.

# Context
Azure Synapse Analytics users can currently connect to Spark using native `spark_connect(..., method = "shell")`. However, this launches a new Spark session even if one is already running. Therefore a new connection method is needed to connect to the existing Spark session. 

Note that on Azure Synapse, there is always a running Spark application when users run `sparklyr` code.

# Implementation Details
1. When an Azure Synapse user executes `spark_connect(..., method = "synapse")`, function `synapse_connection` will be triggered
2. `synapse_connection` first launches the `sparklyr.Shell` and the `sparklyr.Backend` on the existing spark cluster of Azure Synapse, then connects to the cluster by `gateway_connection`
4.  Once the gateway connection is established, `synapse_connection` will query the existing `SparkSession` via `sparklyr` java reflection.
5. All synapse connection functions are organized in a new file `R/synapse_connection.R`.

title: CRAN release prep. Version bump, revdeps refresh, updates news
description:
## On this release:

### Misc

- Addresses new CRAN HTML check NOTEs (https://cran.r-project.org/web/checks/check_results_sparklyr.html.). It also adds a new GHA action to run the 
  same checks to make sure we avoid new issues with this in the future.

### New features

- Adds new metric extraction functions: `ml_metrics_binary()`, 
  `ml_metrics_regression()` and `ml_metrics_multiclass()`. They work closer to 
  how `yardstick` metric extraction functions work. They expect a table with 
  the predictions and actual values, and returns a concise `tibble` with the 
  metrics. (#3281)
  
- Adds new `spark_insert_table()` function. This allows one to insert data into 
  an existing table definition without redefining the table, even when overwriting 
  the existing data. (#3272 @jimhester)

### Bug Fixes

- Restores "validator" functions to regression models. Removing them in a previous
  version broke `ml_cross_validator()` for regression models. (#3273)

### Spark 

- Adds support to Spark 3.3 local installation. This includes the ability to 
  enable and setup log4j version 2. (#3269)

- Updates the JSON file that `sparklyr` uses to find and download Spark for
  local use.  It is worth mentioning that starting with Spark 3.3, the Hadoop
  version number is no longer using a minor version for its download link. So, 
  instead of requesting 3.2, the version to request is 3. 

### Internal functionality

- Removes workaround for older versions of `arrow`. Bumps `arrow` version 
  dependency, from 0.14.0 to 0.17.0 (#3283 @nealrichardson)

- Removes code related to backwards compatibility with `dbplyr`. `sparklyr`
  requires `dbplyr` version 2.2.1 or above, so the code is no longer needed. 
  (#3277)

- Begins centralizing ML parameter validation into a single function that will
  run the proper `cast` function for each Spark parameter.  It also starts using
  S3 methods, instead of searching for a concatenated function name, to find the
  proper parameter validator.  Regression models are the first ones to use this
  new method. (#3279)

- `sparklyr` compilation routines have been improved and simplified.  
  `spark_compile()` now provides more informative output when used.  It also adds
  tests to compilation to make sure. It also adds a step to install Scala in the 
  corresponding GHAs. This is so that the new JAR build tests are able to run. 
  (#3275)

- Stops using package environment variables directly. Any package level variable
  will be handled by a `genv` prefixed function to set and retrieve values.  This
  avoids the risk of having the exact same variable initialized on more than on
  R script. (#3274)

- Adds more tests to improve coverage.

title: Metrics
description: Adds 3 new functions: `ml_metrics_regression()`, `ml_metrics_binary()`, `ml_metrics_multiclass()`. They are similar to `ml_evaluate()`. The difference is that the new functions do not need the original model to process the metrics. They expect a table with the predictions present, preferably from `ml_predict()`.

title: Removes `dbplyr` backwards compatibility code
description:
Since 1.76, `sparklyr` took a hard dependency on `dbplyr` version 2.1.1 or above. This means that backwards compatibility with anything that supports ops is no longer necessary. 

This PR removes the code used to provide support for older versions of `dbplyr` while the transition occurred.  It also add a number of tests to provide better coverage for `dplyr` and `dbplyr` related operations.

By bumping `dbplyr` dependency a big more, to 2.2.1, we are able to remove all of the code switching between "uses ops" and not.

title: Add spark_insert_table function
description:
This allows one to insert data into an existing table definition without
redefining the table, even when overwriting the existing data.

The first test illustrates the problem with the existing method. The existing table definition is ignored by `spark_write_table(mode = "overwrite")`. This causes problems if you are trying to follow best practices of having a table definition defined upfront before writing to it.

Incidentally 88318ab6dfba4ba6e0f0140ec1ada4b45e969e7c should also fix at least one instance of https://github.com/sparklyr/sparklyr/issues/3213, which is caused not by bigints, but because the code currently calls `as.integer(Inf)`, which produces the warning. That commit is tangential to my main purpose of this PR, but thought it worth fixing here anyway.

title: Change `pivot_longer()` argument defaults from `list()` to `NULL`
description:
In tidyr 1.2.0 we updated `pivot_longer()`'s `names_transform`, `values_transform`, `names_ptypes` and `values_ptypes` arguments to allow a _single_ function or ptype which will be applied to all columns, rather than requiring a named list. See https://github.com/tidyverse/tidyr/blob/main/NEWS.md#pivoting

This required us to change the default argument from `list()` to `NULL`. In particular, for `names/values_ptypes`, this was important because `list()` should now be interpreted as "use a list ptype for all columns".

For backwards compatibility with sparklyr and a few other packages that extend `pivot_longer()`, we have temporarily forced `list()` to be interpreted as `NULL`, but we would like to remove this behavior. See https://github.com/tidyverse/tidyr/issues/1296.

This PR is a step towards that by updating the signature used in sparklyr to use `NULL` rather than `list()`. @edgararuiz I forgot to mention this to you before you sent in the sparklyr update, sorry about that. This one is less pressing though.

This may not work out of the box everywhere because you seem to handle these 4 arguments yourself rather than passing on to tidyr. Feel free to copy over the `check_list_of_ptypes()` and `check_list_of_functions()` helpers from tidyr that I added to help standardize these arguments https://github.com/tidyverse/tidyr/blob/60e4f2589e573d38c667a4bbf07822fd5fd9528b/R/pivot-long.R#L243-L244

title: Retools tests
description:
- Replaces ci.yaml GHA with a new, modern, spark-tests.yaml GHA.  This new one properly installs and caches Spark and Livy. It also runs Arrow dev vs Arrow tests properly
- Removed the dependency on `testthat.R` to run tests, everything now goes through the helper and setup files.  
- Updated the PerformanceReporter to only output the summary report, so test output is minimized
- Removed dependency on environment variables to track the Spark connection, and test switches during testing. It is all run through a new.env() variable that tracks settings and the connection
- Removes `context()` from all tests
- Removes the need to use `filter` to run Livy and Arrow Dev related tests. They now are controlled by `skip...` functions that live inside each test script.  This allows us to run Livy tests in interactive RStudio sessions.  We just set the `LIVY_VERSION` env variable, and `devtools::test()` will run the correct tests
- New `setup.R` file in `testthat`. It provides a nice startup message telling us what versions of Spark, Livy and Arrow are being used, and advising that the Spark connections is being opened.  This message will also work during interactive RStudio sessons.
- Adds a separate R CMD Check yaml GHA file that runs `sparklyr` for Windows, Mac and Linux.  R check does not run tests, so this is just to make sure that `sparklyr` does not fail in other OSs
- Updates coverage yaml GHA. It upgrades actions to v2, pre installs Spark, and sets the env variable to force `testthat.R` to run tests.

title: Prepare for the updated `pivot_wider()` signature
description:
CC @edgararuiz

We are planning to release tidyr 1.2.0 this week.

`pivot_wider()` gained 4 new arguments which you can read about [in the NEWS](https://github.com/tidyverse/tidyr/blob/main/NEWS.md#pivoting).

Unfortunately, because of an edge case in the way S3 method registration works, this causes sparklyr to break in revdep checking (in particular, this happens because of the specific combination of S3 issues outlined here https://github.com/DavisVaughan/methodtest).

There isn't anything we can do ahead of time to prevent sparklyr from breaking, but this PR is a first pass at preparing the `pivot_wider()` method for the next release. I've simply added the new arguments and then made them abort if they differ from their default value. Feel free to implement the behavior as you see fit.

Once tidyr is accepted, you should be able to bump the version requirement, remove the Remote, merge this, and then send a patch release to keep sparklyr from being removed from CRAN.

title: Add support for pre-command hooks in the backend
description:
This PR:
* adds support for pre-command hooks in the sparklyr backend, which are intended to be run before handling any method call.  These hooks are set via an overloaded `main` method of sparklyr's `Shell` and are passed as a list of `Runnable` instances.  This will be used by Databricks to support credential passthrough (https://docs.databricks.com/security/credential-passthrough/index.html).
* adds an R unit test to verify that pre-command hooks are successfully executed.  Since there appear to be no framework for testing Scala, I added a method in `backend.scala` intended to only be used for testing.
* fixes various typos
* removes unnecessary and/or legacy code that are no longer needed to support Databricks connections

title: dont check table existence if name randomly generated
description:
This PR proposes to save a call to `spark_remove_table_if_exists()` that is performed on all read operations in the updated functions if the `name` argument is `NULL`. 

If the `name` argument is not user provided (and therefore set to `NULL` by default), the [spark_read_compat_param()](https://github.com/sparklyr/sparklyr/blob/5fb0813ae06df64f8f6ef4d76c0e34d7c96206fc/R/data_interface.R#L24) function will assign a [unique, partially randomly generated](https://github.com/sparklyr/sparklyr/blob/5fb0813ae06df64f8f6ef4d76c0e34d7c96206fc/R/data_interface.R#L5) `name` to the table, meaning that we do not need to check whether the table already exists.

In my testing, this saved somewhere between 1 (for "local") and 8 (in a kubernetes-based stand-alone cluster case) seconds per function call depending on circumstances.

title: Java Version Validation
description:
Since adoption of JEP 223, some Java versions are released only with Major version and no Minor.Security information. In such cases version is shown as X instead of X.0.0, and current regex will not match them.
Also, newer Java versions include a date as part of the version string. We must be able to differentiate numbers from dates from numbers from release, otherwise in some rare cases both version and date will be matched by the current regex resulting in failed validation due to output length.
View issue #1383 for further details.

The proposed change splits the string parsing into 2 steps.
- Trying to match date format (dddd-dd-dd) in the string and filter that out if any match exists (d = digits)
- Match within the remaining results a version in the format of 1 or 2 staring digits followed by zero or one occurrences of '.digit(s).digit(s)' pattern.

title: improvements found while migrating 1b rows perf investigation
description:
While porting the 1b rows perf investigation, found a couple minor issues that are being fixed in this PR. Perhaps the most relevant is that config parameters to the `spark-shell` were not being submitted. Here is a full list of changes:
- Wrap `spark_connect` in a `tryCatch` to remove the global connection reference when connecting fails. This is to enable users to retry when a connection fails.
- Set back the `hive_context` to the connection since it was missing after triggering an idempotent `sc <- spark_connect()`
- Make `dropTempTable` compatible with Spark 2.0.0-preview
- Allow to pass config parameters to the shell with `sparklyr.shell.`. See example in `perf_1b.Rmd`
- Improvement while disconnecting from the shell in cases where stopping the shell fails
- Port and regenerate 1b rows perf investigation

@jjallaire: Safe enough to merge but definitely a review of the changes would be very welcomed.

title: add support for joins against local tables
description:
This PR adds support for joining against local tables. The remaining work here was to allow dplyr to use `copy_to` to transfer the local table into Spark. See example from https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/issues/215:

``` r
n = 1000000
x = data.table(id = 1:n, val = rnorm(n), t = 1:10)
x_spark = sc %>% copy_to(x, overwrite = T)
ts = data.table(t = 1:10, name = letters[1:10])

x_spark %>%
  group_by(t) %>%
  summarize(m = mean(val)) %>%
  arrange(t) %>%
  inner_join(ts, by = c('t'), copy = T)
```

title: Replace ports file with gateway socket
description:
This PR lays the ground work to provide more advanced connection models and removes the need to use an intermediate ports file to ease configuration across platforms.
# current connection architecture

![sparklyr - backend improvements - crop](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/3478847/18896406/536771d6-84d6-11e6-9f1b-13f8c513e7db.png)
- **spark-submit**: When executing spark_connect, sparklyr runs a shell command “spark-submit” which submits the `sparklyr` backend as a jar to Apache Spark..
- **ports-file**: A binary file is written by the sparklyr backend to communicate back to sparklyr the sockets in the backend.
- **socket**: Two sockets are provided, one is a monitor to destroy the backend once it closes, the other one requests java calls and serializes results back.
# improved connection architecture

This PR proposes using the monitor socket as a gateway socket that replaces the ports file and provides routing and reconnection to existing backends as follows:

![sparklyr - new backend - crop](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/3478847/18896493/11b2c956-84d7-11e6-8cc1-04eaa6ed04cc.png)

At this point, it is not intended to add or change functionality. Therefore, commands are expected to work without any additional change.

The only new configuration parameter worth mentioning is the default port the gateway service will attempt to use. In some very particular systems, if this port is already in use, please follow the following configuration pattern:

``` r
config <- spark_config()

# default configuration settings for gateway socket
config[["sparklyr.gateway.port"]] <- "8880"
config[["sparklyr.gateway.address"]] <- "localhost"

sc <- spark_connect(master = "local", config = config)
```

title: implement handling for 'na.action'; default to 'na.omit'
description:
This PR implements handling for a new `ml.option` parameter, `na.action`. This parameter is either an R function, or the name of an R function, and its job is to take a Spark DataFrame, and return a transformed Spark DataFrame (e.g. by dropping missing values, or replacing missing values with 0, and so on.)

This PR also makes the default behavior of `na.action = na.omit`, so that by default missing values are dropped. This change might be contentious, but it should be a good change overall as most Spark.ML methods don't function well with missing values.

We might want to report something like how many values were dropped in such a case, however.

title: Allow use of concurrent connections, `yarn-cluster` regression.
description:
`yarn-cluster` requires connections to be enabled from other cluster machines; first, this can be scoped to only `yarn-cluster` mode, but second, when remote connections are allowed, we only look for one port and if it's not available `sparklyr` fails. Therefore, this issue blocks the following code:

```
sc1 <- spark_connect(master = "local")
sc2 < spark_connect(master = "local", app_name = "other")
```

Added test and enabled allow-remote only for `yarn-cluster`. Tracked by https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/issues/880

title: Attempt to enable code coverage using covr
Improvements to `spark_apply()` for `0.6.1` release
description:
A few improvements to `spark_apply()`:
- **Avoid persisting intermediate data** to disk or memory while using `group_by`: It used to be the case in `0.6` that the RDD was persisting temporarily. The core issue here was a `NullPointerException` triggered in Spark, which further investigation revealed was being caused by iterating over an RDD from a different thread. This is fixed now and paths optimized to avoid any caching.
- **Avoid sampling column types**, it wasn't possible in `0.6` to specify column types to avoid sampling rows form the RDD to create the schema. Now it's possible to run:

```r
iris_tbl %>% spark_apply(
  function(e) e, 
  columns = list(
    Sepal_Length = "double",
    Sepal_Width = "double",
    Petal_Length = "double",
    Petal_Width = "double",
    Species = "character"))
```
- **Fixes two race conditions**: The first one was caused by two or more CPU threads accessing the gateway service which is now fixed by passing the Port of the target backend directly. The second one was lacking support of synchronized `put()` in the JVM object tracker.

Couple minor improvements like simplified debugging and enforce typed `RDD[Row]`

title: Fix windows connection issue with newinstance0 present in logs
description:
Several users have reported a `newinstance0 ` connection issue under Windows. See #98 #229 #277 #295 #354 #397 #409 #456 #466 #497 #633 #679.

I was able to repro this first time `sparklyr` is used in a new environment or by removing `HADOOP_HOME` and relaunching the RStudio.

This issue was being caused by using `SETX` to set the `HADOOP_HOME`. While this would work the next time the rsession launches (and the same session in some other environments); some other environments and packages, say `plumber`, `Conda`, etc. might not respect the `SETX` setting across rsession and trigger this error consistently.

The fix is to set `HADOOP_HOME` during `spark-submit` being specified through `withr::with_envvar`.

There is some risk of regressing scenarios where `SETX` was actually working appropriately. However, given that this has affected multiple Windows users, I think would be best to simplify this and perform an additional change to bring back `SETX` if we find environments where the new approach does not work correctly.

For those users affected by this error, please retry with `sparklyr 0.5.6-9002` or newer. You can install using `devtools::install_github("rstudio/sparklyr")`.

title: Add support for `partition_by` under `spark_write_*` functions
description: Implement support for `partition_by` under `spark_write_*` functions: > Partitioning is one of the most widely used techniques to optimize physical data layout. It provides a coarse-grained index for skipping unnecessary data reads when queries have predicates on the partitioned columns. In order for partitioning to work well, the number of distinct values in each column should typically be less than tens of thousands. For instance, `iris` partitioned over `Species`...

title: Add support for columns parameter in spark_read_* functions to fix #799
description:
Similar to `spark_read_csv()`, add support for `columns` on the other `spark_read_*()` functions, for instance:

```r
spark_read_json(
    sc,name = "iris_json_named",
    path = "test.json",
    columns = c("a", "b", "c")
  )
```

or

```r
spark_read_json(
    sc,name = "iris_json_typed",
    path = "test.json",
```

title: Improve 'argument is of length zero' error and `-Inf` warning while fetching data
description:
Repro:

```r
library(sparklyr)
sc <- spark_connect(master = "local", version = "2.1.0")
DBI::dbGetQuery(sc, "SELECT *")
```

```
Warning message:
In max(n) : no non-missing arguments to max; returning -Inf
```

The problem here is that `max(n)` is invalid for `max(integer(0))`.

The other error is harder to reproduce, see https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/issues/812. But regardless, the `dbFetch` exception is being masked by an error under `ncol(df)` causing:

```
Error in if (ncol(df) > 0) df else invisible(df) : 
  argument is of length zero
```

instead, we should stop earlier to help diagnose issues like this one.

title: Implement R Workers
description: This PR implements support for executing distributed R operations under a new R worker role and adds support for `spark_apply` to transform data frames row-by-row over an arbitrary closure. ## Overview The current architecture of `sparklyr` relies on two components: 1. The **sparklyr client**: Composed of source files under [/r/](https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/tree/master/R) which provide an interface to Spark by establishing and using a connecting to the backend. 2. The **sparklyr backend**: Composed of sources under [/scala/](https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/tree/master/java) which provide support to proxy commands from the client into Spark. So far, this has been enough to provide analysis, machine learning and extensibility capabilities to `sparklyr` since there is a rich set of functionality already implemented into Spark and provided by the Spark community. Additionally, one could write extensions in `sparklyr` with Scala code that would enable arbitrary functionality. However, there are still cases where users would prefer or might require executing specific functionality from R at scale in Spark. This PR implements enable this functionality by providing: 1. Support for `WorkerRDD` that extends Apache Spark `RDD`'s. 2. Support for `spark_apply` to compute a function closure that serializes to the workers. 2. Support for starting an `Rscript` in each `RDD` partition. 3. Support for starting an `sparklyr` backend in each `RDD` partition. 4. Support for connecting back to the backend one the `rscipt` initializes. 5. Support to retrieve the partition, apply the closure and update the results. Notice that a new class of files was introduced prefixed: 1. **worker_**: This prefix indicates that this is code meant to be executed in the worker node with the main function defined as `spark_worker_main`. 2. **core_**: This prefix indicates shared functionality between client and worker. It was explicitly separated under `core_` since absolutely no package dependency can be assumed in this files. So for instance, use of the `config`, `yaml`, `assertthat` or any other package would result in the worker nodes from failing. ## Examples First, some standard initialization: ```{r} library(sparklyr) library(dplyr) sc <- spark_connect(master = "local", version = "2.1.0") iris_tbl <- copy_to(sc, iris) ``` A common distributed computation example is to approximate the value of π. In this case, we will compute whether a point is inside the circle using an R function, but then use `dplyr` to filter and aggregate the results of this approximation: ```{r paged.print=F} sdf_len(sc, 10000) %>% spark_apply(function() sum(runif(2, min = -1, max = 1) ^ 2) < 1) %>% filter(id) %>% count() %>% collect() * 4 / 10000 ``` ``` n 1 3.13 ``` Another example is to apply an R specific function, say`rgamma`, over the a dataset as follows: ```{r} spark_apply(iris_tbl, function(row) { lapply(row[1:4], function(e) e + rgamma(1,2)) }) ``` ``` # Source: table [?? x 4] # Database: spark_connection Sepal_Length Sepal_Width Petal_Length Petal_Width 1 7.676218 6.407721 3.993295 1.4467454 2 10.373125 5.819972 2.933998 1.7986557 3 5.648909 6.097531 3.322528 2.6482938 4 6.807209 3.898670 3.775738 1.9602965 5 9.943737 5.164587 2.282128 1.1904444 6 9.240930 4.492142 3.866824 1.7283005 7 7.814709 3.776937 1.987202 3.9390395 8 7.257176 5.386991 3.768895 3.3914439 9 5.921331 13.847358 2.880484 0.2565747 10 5.993263 4.615195 3.334328 0.8899092 # ... with 140 more rows ``` Notice that `spark_apply` takes the column names of the output data frame but infers them from `colnames(x)`. This works well in the examples above, but one might want to explicitly name the output as follows: ```{r} spark_apply(iris_tbl, function(row) { row$Petal_Width + rgamma(1,2) }, names = "randomized_petal_width") ``` ``` # Source: table [?? x 1] # Database: spark_connection randomized_petal_width 1 2.904409 2 1.788410 3 1.576618 4 2.588035 5 2.808169 6 1.611326 7 1.804285 8 1.106392 9 3.971133 10 2.848165 # ... with 140 more rows ``` One can also retrieve multiple columns in each row by returning a list, and explicitly name the columns in output data frame: ```{r} spark_apply(iris_tbl, function(row) { list(row$Petal_Width + rgamma(1,2), 1) }, names = list("random", "ones")) ``` ``` # Source: table [?? x 2] # Database: spark_connection random ones 1 1.7492575 1 2 0.7582578 1 3 1.3671871 1 4 2.6247821 1 5 4.2132402 1 6 0.6252375 1 7 1.1091248 1 8 1.7231689 1 9 1.7179472 1 10 1.0698262 1 # ... with 140 more rows ``` ## Next steps 1. **Support for packages**. Currently, closures need to be dependency free or alternatively, each worker node needs to be correctly configured with preinstalled libraries. It is obviously a priority to enable this scenario so my plan is to support this soon. 2. **Additional functions**. Other ways of computing arbitrary code that are not strict mappings say by filtering, grouping, etc. Future work will implement those. 3. **Efficient serialization**. It is obvious now that serialization across `sparklyr` client/backend could be significantly improved by using technologies like Apache Arrow or Feather. 4. **R daemon process**. Currently, the`rscript` is launched each time a partition requires computation which has a fixed initialization cost, this could be improved with longed-lived workers.

title: Improve spark_apply performance
description:
Improves `spark_apply` performance, before:

```r
library(sparklyr)
sc <- spark_connect(master = "local")
iris_tbl <- sdf_copy_to(sc, iris)

system.time({
  spark_apply(iris_tbl, function(x) {
    x[1:4] + rgamma(1,2)
  }) %>% collect()
})

  user  system elapsed 
 0.053   0.035  11.128 
```

Now:

```r
system.time({
  spark_apply(highschool_tbl, function(x) {
    x + rgamma(1,2)
  })
})

 user  system elapsed 
0.027   0.004   0.781 
```

SparkR:

```r
library(SparkR)
Sys.setenv(SPARK_HOME = sparklyr::spark_home_dir(version = "2.1.0"))
sparkR.session(master = "local")
iris_tbl <- createDataFrame(iris)

system.time({
  schema <- structType(
    structField("a", "double"),
    structField("b", "double"),
    structField("c", "double"),
    structField("d", "double"))
  collect(
    dapply(iris_tbl, function(x) {
      x[1:4] + rgamma(1,2)
    }, schema)
  )
})

 user  system elapsed 
0.021   0.002   0.257
```

title: Simplify compilation in Windows
description:
See https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/issues/568, which would require the following workarounds to get `compile_package_jars()` working:
 1. Download Scala 2.10 as zip, extract to `Documents/scala`, rename to `scala-2.10`
 2. Download Scala 2.11 as zip, extract to `Documents/scala`, rename to `scala-2.11`
 3. Find `JAVA_HOME` and add `bin` to `PATH` environment variable.

Instead, introducing `download_scalac` do perform (1) and (2) and add support to reuse `JAVA_HOME` which is usually already set while installing `JDK`.

title: Support for dplyr 0.6
description:
Want to write some `dplyr` unit tests before we merge this, so opening this one as WIP. Changes:

 1. `dplyr` now supports `LIMIT` in queries, which allows us to remove our custom code.
 2. `dplyr` not longer requires `USING` which was not supported in `Spark 1.6` and therefore, custom code can be removed.
 3. `mutate` no longer compatible due to `lazyeval` changes, `0.6` will require this change and therefore, this has been backported to this branch https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/commits/bugfix/hotfix-0.5.3 to patch CRAN after `dplyr` releases.
 4. I believe we no longe need `sql_build.tbl_spark`, especially since it gets in the way of triggering `dplyr`'s new query optimizer.

title: Normalize jar paths for windows under spark 1.6
description:
Normalize jar paths for windows under spark 1.6 to fix #491 #490 #414 #410 #398 #305

Planning to backport this one to CRAN, since this is causing a bunch of issues. The problem is scoped to **only** Windows and Spark 1.6.x; however, a lot of users use this configuration since our documentation defaults to 1.6.2.

The fix is straightforward, we need to normalize the paths to jars we specify for the embedded CSV parser. Unfortunately, this affects almost any operation since other non-csv operations also cause Spark to enumerate jar dependencies which trigger an ` java.io.IOException: No FileSystem for scheme` exception.

title: Improve performance for dplyr chains with ml
description:
Perf regression investigation for https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/issues/308, in summary, 4728843 and 591fd31 added valuable functionality to match behavior of `na.action` and to ensure columns are stable across computations; therefore, the computations are needed. Users can avoid the `na.action` functionality by setting `na.action = NULL` in their `ml.options` the other one is required for correct computations.

This PR does improve the case where `na.action` has no side-effect or when it does have a side effect, it caches the output.

The following are perf results for a real `ml_linear_regression` provided by a user over a 260MB partitioned over 200 csv files ran in EMR with a single `m3.xlarge` instance and the data loaded in a S3 bucket.

With `0.4.0` from CRAN:

```
   user  system elapsed 
  1.400   0.144  246.99
```

With master branch this hangs for more than an hour in my particular configuration in EMR.

With master and `na.action = NULL`

```
   user  system elapsed 
  1.936   0.308 373.917 
```

With this PR

```
   user  system elapsed 
  2.060   0.388 478.441 
```

With this PR and `na.action = NULL`

```
   user  system elapsed 
  1.988   0.232 395.106 
```

title: Changes to tbl_cache and sdf_read/write
description:
1. Refactored `tbl_cache` and `tbl_uncache` to not use `dplyr`. This is to allow the non-dplyr features in `sparklyr`  to not require `dplyr`.
 2. Updated documentation to simplify reference guide. For instance, removed `na.replace` and would argue that `dim`, `ncol`, etc. should not be documented since, in the same way that `dplyr` and `DBI` interfaces are not explicitly documented, we shouldn't duplicate documentation. Thoughts welcomed.
 3. Deprecated `sdf_read` and `sdf_write` and provided instead `spark_read` and `spark_write` equivalents to maintain consistency.

title: don't export accessors for sc instance data
improve performance of scala => R object transfer
description:
This PR improves the performance when transferring columns of Spark DataFrames over the wire, by reading the entire column as a large array rather than reading each element one at a time.

Unfortunately, performance is still quite dismal when reading back in large string columns -- I'm not yet sure if we can do much about this (it's tricky as string elements are variable-length, so it's hard to get away from reading one at a time).

One possibility for reading string columns is encoding the entire column as a single byte-array (e.g. with proxy bytes to separate fields, e.g. some non-printable character), and then splitting things back on the R side.

title: ensure `copy_to()` and `collect()` preserve `NA_real_` correctly
description:
After the re-write of `sparklyr` serialization routines, `copy_to()` and `collect()` can now preserve `NA_real_` correctly: `NA_real_` in R becomes `null` in Scala, which gets collected back to R as `NA_real_` (instead being reported incorrectly as `NaN` like it previously was)

Implementation-wise, there is now a custom `Numeric` case class in Scala that maps 1-1 to the `numeric` type in R. It's implemented as a `Option[Double]` with `None` mapping to `NA_real_`, `Some(NaN)` mapping to `NaN`, `Some(<number>)` mapping to `<number>`, etc.

Signed-off-by: Yitao Li <yitao@rstudio.com>

title: rewrite sparklyr serialization routines
description:
- Simplified the serialization code paths significantly; removed the distinction between 'csv_file' and 'csv_string'

title: Add {arrow} to Suggests
description:
When the `arrow` interface was added to `sparklyr`, `arrow` was not yet on CRAN, so the package used some trickery to make it available. Now that `arrow` has been on CRAN for some time (coming up on 10 months), can we make it official?

I broke this PR into a few separate commits, in case you wanted to cherry-pick:

1. Add to `Suggests` and clean up core-arrow.R to use `arrow::` to access functions. I also worked out a solution to #2538 (unrelated) and included it in there in order to reduce churn on the .jar binaries.
2. Simplify the CI setup to use the normal `install.packages()` method for installing Arrow. One job installs from CRAN (or presumably RSPM, which will give you a neat binary), the other from our nightly package repo (bindings have to be compiled from source, but the Arrow C++ library should come as a binary). So this should speed up installation since you won't have to build Arrow C++ from source, and it means you don't have to maintain separate build scripts and cmake configuration for Arrow. This seems like a big win to me.
3. Remove a bunch of `if` statements to work around limitations of the pre-CRAN versions of Arrow and set a minimum version of 0.14, the first that reached CRAN. This makes core-arrow.R very short.
4. Remove some `skip_on_arrow()` for issues that have been fixed and note any open ARROW tickets that correspond to those skips. We can do this more easily now that we're not testing ancient Arrow versions on CI.

title: compare absolute errors instead of relative errors
description:
Because `expect_equal(x, y, tolerance = <epsilon>)` is in most cases checking magnitude of *relative error*, whereas `expect_equal(x, y, tolerance = <max_tolerable_abs_diff>, scale = 1)` will check absolute error (see `?all.equal` for details)

For example, `expect_equal(20, 18, tolerance = 0.1)` => no error reported, because 18 is still within 10% margin of error from 20 whereas `expect_equal(20, 18, tolerance = 0.1, scale = 1)` => error reported because 18 is more than 0.1 away from 20

I shall boldly assume all `expect_equal(x, y, tolerance = <tol>)` incantations are in fact supposed to check for absolute errors (and therefore creating this PR that just appends the required `scale = 1` arg everywhere -- as `scale = 1` to check for absolute error is **not** the default mode of `expect_equal`). If any of these checks are supposed to be checking for relative errors, please suggest change on this PR as soon as possible. 

Signed-off-by: yl790 <yitao@rstudio.com>

title: ml_evaluate() for classification models
description:
I implemented `ml_evaluate` for classification models. Here are examples you can run

```
library(dplyr)
library(sparklyr)

sc <- spark_connect(master = "local", version = "2.3.0")
iris_tbl <- sdf_copy_to(sc, iris, name = "iris_tbl", overwrite = TRUE)

# iris with two species because gbt and svc only support binary classification
iris_tbl_2 <- iris_tbl %>% filter(Species != "setosa")  


iris_tbl %>% 
  ml_naive_bayes(Species ~ .) %>% 
  ml_evaluate(iris_tbl)

iris_tbl %>% 
  ml_random_forest(Species ~ .) %>% 
  ml_evaluate(iris_tbl)

iris_tbl %>% 
  ml_decision_tree(Species ~ .) %>% 
  ml_evaluate(iris_tbl)

iris_tbl %>% 
  ml_multilayer_perceptron_classifier(Species ~ ., layers = c(4,3,3)) %>% 
  ml_evaluate(iris_tbl)

iris_tbl_2%>% 
  ml_gradient_boosted_trees(Species ~ .) %>% # gbt only supports binary classification
  ml_evaluate(iris_tbl_2)

iris_tbl_2 %>% 
  ml_linear_svc(Species ~ .) %>% # svc only supports binary classification
  ml_evaluate(iris_tbl_2)
```

title: Support for partitionId under barrier execution
description:
In order to perform distributed deep learning workflows, one requires to set proper mapping of resources (IPs/ports) to worker ID's, as in `TF_CONFIG`. However, `sparklyr` currently only exposes `address` under the `barrier` parameter in `spark_apply()`, this PR adds support for `partition` to contain the [partitionId](https://spark.apache.org/docs/3.0.0-preview/api/scala/org/apache/spark/BarrierTaskContext.html#partitionId():Int) as well.

Specifically, this enables:

```r
sdf_len(sc, 3, repartition = 3) %>%
  spark_apply(function(df, barrier) {
    as.character(jsonlite::toJSON(barrier))
  }, barrier = TRUE, columns = c(address = "character")) %>%
  collect()
```
```
# A tibble: 3 x 1
  address                                                                                           
  <chr>                                                                                             
1 "{\"partition\":0,\"address\":[\"10.24.202.189:55088\",\"10.44.249.12:50990\",\"10.37.206.225:440…
2 "{\"partition\":1,\"address\":[\"10.24.202.189:55088\",\"10.44.249.12:50990\",\"10.37.206.225:440…
3 "{\"partition\":2,\"address\":[\"10.24.202.189:55088\",\"10.44.249.12:50990\",\"10.37.206.225:440…
```

Notice the new `partition` property in the barrier context.

title: ml_evaluate() for clustering models
description:
Hi, in spark 2.3.0 was implemented Silhouette evaluation for `kmeans`, `bisecting kmeans` and `gmm`, see [here](https://spark.apache.org/docs/2.3.0/ml-clustering.html).
I implemented `ml_evaluate()` for these models. I didn't find any evaluation for `LDA`, so I wrote a warning to this. Here is an example you can run:

```
sc <- spark_connect(master = "local")
iris_tbl <- sdf_copy_to(sc, iris, name = "iris_tbl", overwrite = TRUE)

ml_gaussian_mixture(iris_tbl, Species ~ .) %>%
  ml_evaluate(iris_tbl)

ml_kmeans(iris_tbl, Species ~ .) %>%
  ml_evaluate(iris_tbl)

ml_bisecting_kmeans(iris_tbl, Species ~ .) %>%
  ml_evaluate(iris_tbl)
```

title: revise sparklyr.Utils.collect to read data row-by-row rather than column-by-column
description:
- Main benefit of this change is it gives user an option to avoid calling `df.collect` to fetch the entire data frame onto the driver node. This is done by setting `optimize_mem_util` to true when calling `sdf_collect` (makes sense to do so if the data frame is very large and working on one partition at a time reduces memory footprint at the cost of slightly higher performance overhead)
- Was hoping collecting data row-wise would produce some perf gain as well (because there will likely be more cache locality when working with an array of `Row`s) but so far a number of benchmarks on small and large data frames showed this change appear to be performance-neutral. A bit surprised by it TBH. Either there wasn't really a lot more cache hits, or the increased cache hits did not figure prominently in overall perf numbers due to other larger overheads.
- Still need to update jar files on the livy branch to fix livy test failures from this change -- ignore livy test failures for now
- Bonus point: this change allows us to avoid all the `local.map{row => { ... }` boilerplate code in many places. So, code-readability improved a bit as well : ) Yay.

Signed-off-by: yl790 <yitao@rstudio.com>

title: Fix summary() in ml_linear_regression when intercept = FALSE
description:
This PR is related to #2230

Here is an example that you can run 
```
library(dplyr)
library(sparklyr)

sc <- spark_connect(master = "local")

# copy mtcars into spark
mtcars_tbl <- copy_to(sc, 
                      df = mtcars, 
                      overwrite = TRUE)

  # fit LM with intercept 
  fit_with_intercept <- mtcars_tbl %>%
  ml_linear_regression(mpg ~ wt + cyl, 
                       fit_intercept = TRUE) # param set to TRUE (default)

# fit LM without intercept 
fit_without_intercept <- mtcars_tbl %>%
  ml_linear_regression(mpg ~ wt + cyl,
                       fit_intercept = FALSE) # param set to FALSE 
```

title: Allow sdf_query_plan to also get analyzed plan
description:
Allow sdf_query_plan to also get analyzed plan, which is more useful for DB Connect. The PR adds an optional argument to `sdf_query_plan`, to get either the optimized or analyzed plan. When called with DB Connect, the optimized plan is just a LogicalRemoteExec "black box", and doesn't display much useful query information. Instead, the analyzed plan can be used to examine the query. 

For backwards compatibility, the `plan_type` argument of `sdf_query_plan` defaults to `optimizedPlan`, so that existing usage will have the same behavior.

This also fixes and enables two tests for DB Connect that check query plans.

title: WIP: Support for copy_to() in databricks connection
description:
Currently, `copy_to()` does not work with `spark_connect(master = "local", method = "databricks")`, spotted by @blairj09.

The problem is that [the selection of the data serializer](https://github.com/sparklyr/sparklyr/blob/cf3f4d6e5f56856aa4f25fe887190c11b2090c8a/R/data_copy.R#L227) currently assumes the databricks connection runs in the driver node, which is not the case. Moving the check for `databrick-connect` to `spark_connection_is_local()` fixes this issue and potentially fixes (or breaks!) other code paths. I took a look at the code and I believe this is the right fix, but we should definitely wait for tests to pass.

Notice also that, in theory, if `arrow` is installed in the databricks cluster, `copy_to()` should work and be so much faster than the standard implementation.

title: Improve serialization and deserialization of date and timestamp types
description:
This PR addresses the issue in https://github.com/sparklyr/sparklyr/issues/2314

- Turns out previously 1970-01-01 00:00:00 UTC was being used as a sentinel value to represent NA in `core_deserializer.R`, which was not good because it would cause an actual timestamp / date type with value 1970-01-01 00:00:00 UTC to be non-representable after being collected from Spark to R -- A more concrete example, let's say I'm working with very long term historic data such as `ggplot2::economics`, then I could end up with employment rates from year 1968, 1969, NA, 1971, etc after collecting my date from Spark to R, which would definitely be weird. In fact, that was how I found this bug.
- It feels like the `timeNA` hack in `core_deserializer.R` was actually trying to "cancel out" a bunch of other bugs in `utils.scala`, but introduced undesired side-effects. So, this PR tries to address the acutal issue in `utils.scala` instead, and reverts the hacky change in `core_deserializer.R`.

Signed-off-by: Yitao Li <yitao@rstudio.com>

title: Improve collect() performance for columns with lists
description:
Currently,

```r
library(sparklyr)
sc <- spark_connect(master = "local")

list(list(g = 1, d = 1:5000), list(g = 2, d = 1:5000)) %>%
    jsonlite::write_json(temp_json, auto_unbox = T)

nested <- spark_read_json(sc, temp_json, memory = FALSE)

system.time(collected <- collect(nested))
```
```
   user  system elapsed 
  6.542   0.087   6.826 
```

This is happening since list entries require `sparklyr` to ask each element from the backend one at a time, with this improvement:

```r
system.time(collected <- collect(nested))
```
```
   user  system elapsed 
  9.804   0.273   0.310 
```

To install this fix before this PR is merged use the following command and restart your R session:

```
remotes::install_github("sparklyr/sparklyr", ref = "bugfix/collect-nested-perf")
```

title: Basic support in 'copy_to()' for data frames with list columns

DataFrames with list-columns can't currently be copied to Spark using `copy_to()`, since the structure is arbitrary, this fix transforms them to JSON columns to unblock the copy operation.

```r
library(sparklyr)
sc <- spark_connect(master = "local")

dfjson <- tibble::tibble(
    g = c(1, 2, 3),
    data = list(
      tibble::tibble(x = 1, y = 2),
      tibble::tibble(x = 4:5, y = 6:7),
      tibble::tibble(x = 10)
    )
)

dfjson <- copy_to(sc, dfjson, overwrite = TRUE)
dfjson
```
```
# Source: spark<dfjson> [?? x 2]
      g data                                   
  <dbl> <chr>                                  
1     1 "[{\"x\":1,\"y\":2}]"                  
2     2 "[{\"x\":4,\"y\":6},{\"x\":5,\"y\":7}]"
3     3 "[{\"x\":10}]"
```

One can then use `get_json_object()` to retrieve the content,

```r
dfjson %>% dplyr::mutate(data = get_json_object(data, "$[0].x"))
```
```
# Source: spark<?> [?? x 2]
      g data 
  <dbl> <chr>
1     1 1    
2     2 4    
3     3 10   
```

title: Deprecate Livy source-uploads to favor using JARs
description:
Earlier versions of sparklyr supported connecting to Livy as:

```r
sc <- spark_connect(
  master = "https://domain/livy/",
  method = "livy",
  config = livy_config(user = "<user>", password = "<password>"))
```

Since the Spark version was unknown, this would cause `sparklyr` to connect, check the Spark version, and then upload all correct sources to Livy (see [inst/livy/](https://github.com/sparklyr/sparklyr/tree/feature/sparklyr-1.0/inst/livy/)), which at the time was useful to ensure connectivity to any Livy instance.

However, in order to support this source-based upload to Livy, the `sparklyr` backend code had to be written to be serializable. This was OK in early versions, but as the codebase evolved, we had to add additional workarounds, like declaring imports within a class, see [channel.scala#L5-L20](https://github.com/sparklyr/sparklyr/blob/feature/sparklyr-1.0/java/spark-1.5.2/channel.scala#L5-L20).

To help others contribute with ease to `sparklyr`, this PR deprecates this embedded Livy sources connection method and enforces using the `version` parameter in Livy connections for `spark_connect()`, a feature introduced in `sparklyr 1.0`. This is also desirable since it's much faster to use Livy with a precompiled JAR than uploading sources.

New Livy connections are now expected to be initialized with the `version` parameter; otherwise, an error will be presented to the user:

```r
sc <- spark_connect(
  master = "https://domain/livy/",
  version = "2.3.1",
  method = "livy",
  config = livy_config(user = "<user>", password = "<password>"))
```

This PR does ALSO cleans up the `scala` sources, by refactoring the imports and also avoiding `invoke()` calls.

title: Allow passing verbatim spark.sql.types as column definitions in spark_read_
description:
Related to https://github.com/sparklyr/sparklyr/pull/2219, this proposes to allow passing verbatim `spark.sql.types` when using the columns argument. This 
- can be useful for instance when storing the target object schemas (retrieved for example with `sdf_schema()`) elsewhere.
- also removes the need of actually investigating the mapping from "R types" to `spark.sql.types`.

Also added some unit tests to test both the new and legacy functionality.

Note on compilation:
- I was not able to recompile the sources for Spark version < 2.0.0 possibly due to `SparkSession` (which IIRC was introduced only with Spark 2.0) being used in other, untouched sources. Recompiled for `targets = c("2.0.0", "2.3.0", "2.4.0")` for now.

title: Include barrier in spark_apply
description:
I added barrier to spark_apply, but there are some points to discuss:

- Pass `columns` parameter to spark_apply ( error in `schema <- spark_schema_from_rdd(sc, rdd, columns)`)
- `sdf_register` gives an error when use barriers, that is why I use `invoke("collect") in the end
- `worker_log_env$sessionId` is `NULL`, that is why `spark_log(sc, filter = "IPs:")` returns nothing

Here is an example you can run
```
sc <- spark_connect(master = "local[3]")
sdf_len(sc, 3, repartition = 3) %>% 
  spark_apply(nrow, barrier = TRUE, columns = c(id = "integer")) %>% 
  invoke("collect")

```

title: Add support in spark_apply() for context param
description:
Currently, all closures in `spark_apply()` need to be self-contained and therefore, the following operation is not supported:

```r
a <- 1
spark_apply(sdf_len(sc, 1), function(e) {
    e + a
})
```

To mitigate this and support similar use cases, this PR adds a new `context` parameter to pass an additional object, as in:

```r
spark_apply(sdf_len(sc, 1), function(e, c) {
    e + c
}, context = 1)
```
```
# Source:   table<sparklyr_tmp_174e249c63036> [?? x 1]
# Database: spark_connection
     id
  <dbl>
1     2
```

Or even a function, etc...

```r
spark_apply(sdf_len(sc, 1), function(e, c) {
    e + c(1, 1)
}, context = function(a, b) { a + b })
```
```
# Source:   table<sparklyr_tmp_174e21157de2e> [?? x 1]
# Database: spark_connection
     id
  <dbl>
1     3
```

title: Do not use temporary directory in testthat_shell_connection
description:
I tried to run a specific test using:
```
$ R
> library(devtools)
> test_file('tests/testthat/test-feature-vector-indexer.R')
```
This didn't work because `testthat_spark_connection()` sets the working directory to a temporary directory, and then when [this line](https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/blob/master/tests/testthat/test-feature-vector-indexer.R#L22) attempts to find a file within `getwd()`, it cannot find the data file in the temporary directory.

Can we remove the code that sets the working directory to a temp directory? Or, is there any other way I can run this individual test without patching the code? My current workaround is to run `test_file('tests/testthat/test-feature-vector-indexer.R')` twice: it fails the first time, but because the spark connection has been set up already, it passes the second time. 

I am not sure how this affects other tests, so I'll keep an eye on the CI.

title: support sparklyr executor memory setting and warn to fix printed book issue
description:
The printed version of Spark with R book suggests connecting in YARN as:

```
# Memory in Driver
config["sparklyr.shell.driver-memory"] <- "2g"

# Memory per Worker
config["sparklyr.executor.memory"] <- "2G" 

# Cores per Worker
config["sparklyr.shell.executor-cores"] <- 1

# Number of Workers
config["sparklyr.shell.num-executors"] <- 3
```

which is honestly kinda intuitive since one is specifying all settings with `sparklyr` prefix; however, this is incorrect. To help out users, we will support `sparklyr.shell.executor-cores`, but warn users this is the incorrect setting.

title: Allow reading multiple files with `spark_read_`
description:
Some of the `org.apache.spark.sql.DataFrameReader` methods allow for passing `paths: String*`, besides `path: String`. We can use this to allow the `spark_read_` suite of functions to accept multiple paths, not just a single path and read multiple files in one call (inspired in part by [SO question](https://stackoverflow.com/q/57531647/8876652)).

This PR proposes to add this support to:

- `spark_read_parquet()`
- `spark_read_json()`
- `spark_read_text()` - with `whole=FALSE` only, stops with a meaningful error message if multiple paths are provided with `whole=TRUE`
- `spark_read_orc()`

Unit tests are also added for the above reading functions.

Compatibility notes on [DataFrameReader](https://spark.apache.org/docs/2.3.0/api/scala/index.html#org.apache.spark.sql.DataFrameReader) supporting `paths: String*`:

- `.parquet` - since 1.4.0 
- `.json` - since 2.0.0
- `.text` - since 1.6.0
- `.orc` - since 2.0.0

title: Support for Kubernetes
description: [Add support for Kubernetes](https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/issues/1525#issuecomment-404964718): ```r sc <- spark_connect(config = spark_config_kubernetes("k8s://192.168.99.100:8443")) ``` ## Work Items - [x] Use deterministic ports to allow kubernetes port forwarding. - [x] Support to set up port forwarding automatically - [x] Simplify required `spark_config()` options ## Minikube Use minikube to run Kubernetes locally with sparklyr as follows: - Install the [kubernetes-cli](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/tools/install-kubectl/) and [minikube](https://github.com/kubernetes/minikube/releases), from OS X you can run: `brew install kubernetes-cli minikube`. - Run `minikube start` as described in the [quickstart](https://kubernetes.io/docs/setup/minikube/#quickstart) - Ensure enough resources are assigned to minikube, for instance, `minikube stop`, modify VirtualBox to use 4 CPUs and 4Gb, rerun `minikube start`. - Get the master address by running `kubectl cluster-info`. - Create a `sparklyr` folder in `SPARK_HOME` and copy the `sparklyr` jars from `system.file("java", package = "sparklyr")`. - Modify the Spark `kubernetes/dockerfiles/spark/Dockerfile` to create a `/opt/sparklyr` path and copy the `sparklyr` jars. For instance by adding `mkdir -p /opt/sparklyr && \` and `COPY sparklyr /opt/sparklyr`. - To prevent `Forbidden!Configured service account doesn't have access` [generate service account](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/49152771/kubernetes-1-9-cant-initialize-sparkcontext): `kubectl create serviceaccount spark` and `$ kubectl create clusterrolebinding spark-role --clusterrole=edit --serviceaccount=default:spark --namespace=default`. - Generate the cluster [docker images](https://github.com/apache/spark/blob/master/docs/running-on-kubernetes.md#docker-images) by running from SPARK_HOME: `./bin/docker-image-tool.sh -m -t sparklyr build`. However, you might hit an error with a workaround available in [this](https://iamninad.com/running-spark-job-on-kubernetes-minikube/) post. ## Notes Notice that `spark_config_kubernetes()` is just a convenience function that could be replaced by something like: ```r sc <- spark_connect( master = "k8s://https://192.168.99.100:8443", config = list( sparklyr.shell.master = "k8s://https://192.168.99.100:8443", "sparklyr.shell.deploy-mode" = "cluster", sparklyr.gateway.remote = TRUE, sparklyr.shell.name = "sparklyr", sparklyr.shell.class = "sparklyr.Shell", sparklyr.shell.conf = c( "spark.kubernetes.container.image=spark:sparklyr", "spark.kubernetes.driver.pod.name=spark-driver", "spark.kubernetes.authenticate.driver.serviceAccountName=spark" ), sparklyr.app.jar = "local:///opt/sparklyr/sparklyr-2.3-2.11.jar", sparklyr.events.aftersubmit = function() { # wait for pods to launch Sys.sleep(15) # configure port forwarding system2( "kubectl", c("port-forward", "spark-driver", "8880:8880", "8881:8881", "4040:4040"), wait = FALSE ) } ), spark_home = spark_home_dir() ) ```

title: Livy performance improvement by using sparklyr JARs
description:
This change speeds up Livy operations by 6X for `spark_connect()`, 3X for `copy_to()` and other operations around 5X. Improves: https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/issues/1865 and https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/issues/741.

### Using Sources

```r
livy_service_start()
system.time(sc <- spark_connect(master = "http://localhost:8998", method = "livy"))
```
```
   user  system elapsed 
  4.531   0.536 141.961 
```
```r
system.time(iris_tbl <- sdf_copy_to(sc, iris))
```
```
   user  system elapsed 
  2.697   0.302  59.991 
```
```
system.time(m <- ml_linear_regression(iris_tbl, Petal_Width ~ Petal_Length))
```
```
   user  system elapsed 
 11.036   0.962 230.123 
```

### Using JARs

```r
config <- livy_config(spark_version = "2.3.0")
system.time(sc <- spark_connect(master = "http://localhost:8998", method = "livy", config = config))
```
```
   user  system elapsed 
  1.351   0.080  21.977
```

```r
system.time(iris_tbl <- sdf_copy_to(sc, iris))
```
```
   user  system elapsed 
  2.390   0.116  21.486
```
```
system.time(m <- ml_linear_regression(iris_tbl, Petal_Width ~ Petal_Length))
livy_service_stop()
```
```
   user  system elapsed 
  7.935   0.316  43.098 
```

Notice the connection code is equivalent to the one bellow since the `spark_version` parameter finds and sets the `jars` parameter for you; however, others might want to copy the `sparklyr` into HDFS and list this JAR explicitly.

```
config <- livy_config(
  jars = "https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/blob/bugfix/livy-jars/inst/java/sparklyr-2.3-2.11.jar?raw=true",
  sources = FALSE
)
sc <- spark_connect(master = "http://localhost:8998", method = "livy", config = config)
```

title: Support parameters in spark-submit
description:
This PR adds support fo parse command line parameters in `spark-submit`. For instance, for the following `batch.R` file:

```r
library(sparklyr)
sc <- spark_connect(master = "local")

copy_to(sc, data.frame(params = commandArgs(trailingOnly = TRUE))) %>%
  spark_write_text("params.txt")

spark_disconnect(sc)
```

This can be submitted as:

```bash
/spark-home-path/bin/spark-submit --files batch.R --class sparklyr.Shell
  --master local '/sparklyr-jars-path/sparklyr-2.3-2.11.jar'
  8880 12345 --batch batch.R some-parameter=10
```

which will produce the following file in Spark:

```
8880
12345
--batch
batch.R
some-parameter=10
```

To retrieve a particular parameter, say `some-parameter`, the R script can be modified to retrieve this parameter with custom code, for instance:

```r
strsplit(args[grepl("some-parameter", args)], "=")[[1]][2]
```

title: Support for Copying and Collecting Batches
description:
Support uploading/collecting larger datasets:
- [x] Support to upload RDD batches.
- [x] Support to collect RDD batches.

# Batched Copy

```r
write.csv(iris, "iris/iris1.csv", row.names = F)
write.csv(iris, "iris/iris2.csv", row.names = F)
write.csv(iris, "iris/iris3.csv", row.names = F)

library(sparklyr)
sc <- spark_connect(master = "local")

# upload batches using callback
iris_tbl <- sdf_copy_to(
  sc,
  lapply(dir("iris", full.names = T), function(path) function() read.csv(path)),
  overwrite = T)

# upload batches using rlang expression
iris_tbl <- sdf_copy_to(
  sc,
  lapply(dir("iris", full.names = T), function(path) ~read.csv(path)),
  overwrite = T)

# upload batches using flowery generator
library(flowery)
iris_tbl <- sdf_copy_to(
  sc,
  generator({
    for (path in dir("iris", full.names = T)) yield(read.csv(path))
  }),
  overwrite = T)
```

# Batched Collection

```r
library(sparklyr)

sc <- spark_connect(master = "local")
sdf_len(sc, 10, repartition = 2) %>%
  collect(callback = function(df) message("Collecting ", nrow(df), " rows."))
```

title: Unique SqlContext per databricks connection
description:
In databricks we create a unique SqlContext (HiveContext) for each notebook or rstudio session even though all users share the same spark context. Because sparklyr uses getOrCreate to get the SqlContext for each user, our users end up sharing a SqlContext. This has causes unexpected behavior and errors for our sparklyr users.

This PR allows databricks connections to get the right SqlContext upfront, resolving this issue.

```
> class(ml_logistic_regression(sc))
[1] "ml_logistic_regression"      "ml_probabilistic_classifier"
[3] "ml_classifier"               "ml_predictor"               
[5] "ml_estimator"                "ml_pipeline_stage"  
```

title: Implement Arrow
description: Support for Apache Arrow in `sparklyr`. ```r # Install this PR devtools::install_github("apache/arrow", subdir = "r", ref = "dc5df8f") devtools::install_github("rstudio/sparklyr") # Initialize Data df <- data.frame(y = runif(10^5, 0, 1)) # Initialize sparklyr library(sparklyr) sc <- spark_connect(master = "local", version = "2.3.1") ``` # Benchmarks For completeness, adding `sparkR`, which gets initialized as: ``` # Initialize SparkR Sys.setenv(SPARK_HOME = sparklyr::spark_home_dir("2.3.1")) library(SparkR, lib.loc = c(file.path(Sys.getenv("SPARK_HOME"), "R", "lib"))) sess <- sparkR.session(master = "local[*]") ``` ## Copying ```r copy_benchmark <- microbenchmark::microbenchmark( arrow = { library(arrow) sparklyr_df <<- dplyr::copy_to(sc, df, memory = T, overwrite = T) dplyr::count(sparklyr_df) }, sparklyr = { if ("arrow" %in% .packages()) detach("package:arrow") sparklyr_df <<- dplyr::copy_to(sc, df, memory = T, overwrite = T) dplyr::count(sparklyr_df) }, sparkr = { sparkr_df <<- SparkR::cache(SparkR::as.DataFrame(df)) SparkR::count(sparkr_df) }, times = 10 ) ggplot2::autoplot(copy_benchmark) ``` ![copy-benchmark](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/3478847/47053697-fd366200-d162-11e8-80a4-d08e71238a0f.png) ## Collecting ```r collect_benchmark <- microbenchmark::microbenchmark( arrow = { library(arrow) sparklyr_local <<- dplyr::collect(sparklyr_df) }, sparklyr = { if ("arrow" %in% .packages()) detach("package:arrow") sparklyr_local <<- dplyr::collect(sparklyr_df) }, sparkr = { sparkr_local <<- collect(sparkr_df) }, times = 10 ) ggplot2::autoplot(collect_benchmark) ``` ![collect-benchmark](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/3478847/47051540-79c44300-d159-11e8-8c87-2afa884ea2ae.png) Running this benchmark with `10^6` entries shows improvements under `arrow`, ```r df_large <- data.frame(y = runif(10^6, 0, 1)) sparklyr_large <<- dplyr::copy_to(sc, df_large, memory = T, overwrite = T) collect_large_benchmark <- microbenchmark::microbenchmark( arrow = { library(arrow) sparklyr_local <<- dplyr::collect(sparklyr_large) }, sparklyr = { if ("arrow" %in% .packages()) detach("package:arrow") sparklyr_local <<- dplyr::collect(sparklyr_large) }, times = 10 ) ggplot2::autoplot(collect_large_benchmark) ``` ![collect-large-benchmark](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/3478847/47052505-83e84080-d15d-11e8-8c0e-478f9cea97a5.png) ## spark_apply() ```r r_benchmark <- microbenchmark::microbenchmark( arrow = { library(arrow) spark_apply(sparklyr_df, ~ .x / 1.2, columns = list(x = "numeric"), env = list(R_ENABLE_JIT = "0"), memory = F) %>% dplyr::count() %>% dplyr::collect() }, sparklyr = { if ("arrow" %in% .packages()) detach("package:arrow") spark_apply(sparklyr_df, ~ .x / 1.2, columns = list(x = "numeric"), memory = F) %>% dplyr::count() %>% dplyr::collect() }, sparkr = { dapply(sparkr_df, function(x) x / 1.2, structType(structField("y", "double"))) %>% SparkR::count() }, times = 10, control = list(order = "block") ) ggplot2::autoplot(r_benchmark) ``` ![r-benchmark](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/3478847/47120230-bf990e00-d222-11e8-9391-78598ef60413.png) Notice that [JIT](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/compiler/html/compile.html) was turned off since it adds a bit of overhead in `spark_apply()` for this particular example, here is a detailed comparison between JIT enabled/disabled with `arrow`: ```r jit_benchmark <- microbenchmark::microbenchmark( jit_off = { library(arrow) spark_apply(sparklyr_df, ~ .x / 1.2, columns = list(x = "numeric"), env = list(R_ENABLE_JIT = "0"), memory = F) %>% dplyr::count() %>% dplyr::collect() }, jit_on = { library(arrow) spark_apply(sparklyr_df, ~ .x / 1.2, columns = list(x = "numeric"), memory = F) %>% dplyr::count() %>% dplyr::collect() }, times = 10 ) ggplot2::autoplot(jit_benchmark) ``` ![jit-benchmark](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/3478847/47120222-b9a32d00-d222-11e8-86bc-abad9d5b40a9.png) [Here is a profile](http://rpubs.com/jluraschi/spark-apply-profile-arrow) measuring time spent while running `spark_apply()`, loading `arrow` seems to take `260ms` which could be worth investigating further at some point: Comparing with `scala`: ```scala def time[R](block: => R): R = { val t0 = System.currentTimeMillis() val result = block // call-by-name val t1 = System.currentTimeMillis() println("Elapsed time: " + (t1 - t0) + "ms") result } val data = spark.range(1,100000,1).cache time { data.map(_ / 1.2).count() } Elapsed time: 174ms res16: Long = 99999 ``` ## Tests From the Travis run performance results, we can compare execution against arrow as follows: ```r library(dplyr) data_sparklyr <- read.csv("~/RStudio/temp/sparklyr-perf-tests-spark.txt") %>% pull() %>% stringr::str_match(., "(.*) ([0-9]+\\.?[0-9]*)") %>% as.data.frame() %>% transmute(test = trimws(V2), serializer = "sparklyr", time = as.numeric(trimws(V3))) data_arrow <- read.csv("~/RStudio/temp/sparklyr-perf-tests-arrow.txt") %>% pull() %>% stringr::str_match(., "(.*) ([0-9]+\\.?[0-9]*)") %>% as.data.frame() %>% transmute(test = trimws(V2), serializer = "arrow", time = as.numeric(trimws(V3))) library(ggplot2) bind_rows(data_sparklyr, data_arrow) %>% ggplot(aes(x=test, y=time, fill = serializer)) + geom_bar(stat='identity', position='dodge') + theme(axis.text.x = element_blank(), axis.ticks.x=element_blank()) ``` ![sparklyr-arrow-tests](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/3478847/47690198-57dfad00-dbaa-11e8-859d-dcdf372b770e.png) ```r bind_rows(data_sparklyr, data_arrow) %>% tidyr::spread(serializer, time) %>% summarise(arrow = sum(arrow), sparklyr = sum(sparklyr)) ``` ``` arrow sparklyr 1 1406.354 1475.308 ``` Overall, `arrow` tests execute faster than the `sparklyr` serializer, Travis tests use only small datasets but help ensure unnecessary overhead is not being introduced.
