title: Support for tables with periods
description:
```r
sensors <- data.frame(
    sensor = c("s.ensor@1", "s.ensor@1","s.ensor@1","s.ensor@2","s.ensor@2","s.ensor@2"),
    time = c(1,2,3,1,2,3),
    metric = c(1,2,3,10,20,30)
)

sc <- spark_connect(master = "local")

sensors_tbl <- sdf_copy_to(sc, sensors, overwrite = T)

sensors_tbl %>%
  sdf_pivot(time ~ sensor, fun.aggregate = c("avg", "metric")) %>%
  select(`s.ensor@1`)
```

```
# Source: spark<?> [?? x 1]
  `s.ensor@1`
*       <dbl>
1           1
2           3
3           2
```

Consider using instead [dbplyr::in_schema(database, table)](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/dbplyr/versions/1.2.2/topics/in_schema) instead.

This can also be reverted to match previous versions through:

```r
sc <- spark_connect(master = "local", config = list(sparklyr.dplyr.period.splits = T))
sensors_tbl <- sdf_copy_to(sc, sensors, overwrite = T)

sensors_tbl %>%
  sdf_pivot(time ~ sensor, fun.aggregate = c("avg", "metric")) %>%
  select(`s.ensor@1`) %>% dbplyr::sql_render()
```
```
<SQL> SELECT `s`.`ensor@1`
FROM `sparklyr_tmp_f23019c81436`
```

Current workaround:

```r
sensors_tbl %>%
  mutate(sensor = regexp_replace(sensor, "\\\\.", "_")) %>%
  sdf_pivot(time ~ sensor, fun.aggregate = c("avg", "metric")) %>%
  select(`s_ensor@1`)
```
```
# Source: spark<?> [?? x 1]
  `s_ensor@1`
*       <dbl>
1           1
2           3
3           2
```

title: spark_connect() should not attempt to download version data

Found a case while connecting using Spark 2.3.1 (which just recently got added), in which `spark_connect()` would attempt to download the versions and fail since the version 2.3.1 was not int he versions file.

Fixed the original issue but more importantly, `spark_connect()` should never rely on the remote versions file to make sure that, even if we make a bad commit to the versions file, we wouldn't affect users workflow in `spark_connect()` but rather, only while using `spark_install()`.

title: [WIP] Don't force index numeric labels for classification
description:
Fixes https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/issues/1591

@shabbybanks I cherry-picked your test from https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/pull/1598 and it seems to be passing at least locally. Please give this a shot and propose more tests as needed.

The use case that this change would break is where the labels are two distinct integers that are not 0 and 1, e.g.

```
library(sparklyr)
library(dplyr)
sc <- spark_connect(master = "local")
train_data <- iris %>%
  mutate(
    species_type = ifelse(Species == "setosa", 2, 1),
  )
spark_data <- copy_to(sc, train_data, "like_iris", overwrite = TRUE)
s_mod <- spark_data %>%
  ml_logistic_regression(formula = species_type ~ Sepal_Length)
s_mod
# Formula: species_type ~ Sepal_Length
# 
# Coefficients:
#      (Intercept) Sepal_Length
# [1,]   -3.455491 -5.161826758
# [2,]  -12.186625  5.168782843
# [3,]   15.642117 -0.006956085
```

but this is arguably less likely than users being misled by 0 and 1 being mapped to 1 and 0.

Will add a NEWS entry before merge that makes this behavior clear.

title: Broom for naive bayes and logistic regression
description:
Hi @javierluraschi,

I've done tidy(), augment() and glance() for naive bayes and logistic regression.
I realized that augment() code will be the same for supervised models and the only difference is the column name .prediction (for regression) and .predicted_label (for classification). Because of this, I created a function named broom_augment_supervised() inside the utils_tidier.R. This function verify the model's class and put the appropriate name inside augment() data.frame.

Here is the code you can run:

```
library(sparklyr)
sc <-  spark_connect(master = "local", version = "2.2.1")
iris_tbl <- sdf_copy_to(sc, iris, name = "iris_tbl", overwrite = TRUE)

# logistic regression (binary classification)
iris_tbl %>%
  dplyr::filter(Species != "setosa") %>% 
  ml_logistic_regression(Species ~ .) %>% 
  tidy()

# logistic regression (multiclass classification)
iris_tbl %>%
  ml_logistic_regression(Species ~ .) %>% 
  tidy()

# naive bayes (multiclass classification)
iris_tbl %>%
  ml_naive_bayes(Species ~ .) %>% 
  tidy()

# logistic regression with new data
iris_tbl %>%
  ml_logistic_regression(Species ~ .) %>% 
  augment(head(iris_tbl,25))

# naive bayes without newdata
iris_tbl %>%
  ml_naive_bayes(Species ~ .) %>% 
  augment()

# decision_tree (classification)
iris_tbl %>% 
  ml_decision_tree(Species ~ ., seed = 123) %>% 
  augment()

# decision_tree (regression)
iris_tbl %>% 
  ml_decision_tree(Sepal_Length ~ Petal_Length + Petal_Width, seed = 123) %>% 
  augment()

# logistic regression
iris_tbl %>%
  ml_logistic_regression(Species ~ .) %>% 
  glance()

iris_tbl %>%
  ml_naive_bayes(Species ~ .) %>% 
 glance()
```

title: Fix Hive support in Spark 2.3
description:
- `spark_connect()` now first initializes a `SparkSession` before obtaining a `SparkContext` from it. This is required in order to properly set the static SQL configs such as `spark.sql.catalogImplementation`. The `SparkSession` is immediately cached as the `hive_context` field.
- Default `spark.sql.catalogImplementation` to `hive` so Hive support is enabled. Users can opt out of this by setting the option to `in-memory`.
- `spark_version()` now actually caches the Spark version in the connection object.

Closes https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/issues/1496, closes https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/issues/415

title: Improvements when Spark shut downs with OutOfMemory
description: When Spark shut downs with `OutOfMemory` exception, the connection closes and a few side effects trigger in `sparklyr`. The most prominent problem is calling multiple times `cancelAllJobs` which will fail multiple times, additionally, fixing multiple creations of hive context due to delayed creation and missing to register in all connection objects.

title: ML internals refactoring
description:
## ML
- Construction of pipeline stages now uses standard evaluation. This was changed in preparation of the developer API feature, since there was too much magic going on that would be difficult to reason about.
- **(Breaking change)** For model objects, `lazy val` and `def` attributes have been converted to closures, so they are not evaluated at object instantiation. Fixes https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/issues/1453.
- Input and output column names are no longer required to construct pipeline objects to be consistent with Spark. Fixes https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/issues/1513.
- Vector attributes of pipeline stages are now printed correctly, fixes https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/issues/1618.
- Soft deprecate various aliases favoring method names in Spark.

## Miscellaneous
- Tests default to using Spark 2.3.0.
- Import **purrr** for better maintainability.
- Use [**forge**](https://github.com/kevinykuo/forge) for input value checking for the time being. Will evaluate https://github.com/r-lib/vctrs as it develops and decide what we recommend to sparklyr extension authors.

title: Implement spark streaming
description: This PR adds support for structured streaming in `sparklyr`. Streams are constructed by reading from a streaming source and writing into a streaming source, the simplest stream can be defined as follows: ```r stream_read_csv(sc, "iris-in") %>% stream_write_csv("iris-out") ``` However, `dplyr`, pipelines, `SQL` and `spark_apply()` are also supported. **dplyr:** `dplyr` pipelines can be constructed by piping the streaming source into `dplyr` and then writing the `dplyr` transformation to the output stream: ```r stream_read_csv(sc, "iris-in") %>% summarise(n = n()) %>% stream_write_csv("iris-out") ``` **pipelines:** Spark pipelines can only be used for scoring, first fit a pipeline, then use it under streaming as follows: ```r fitted_pipeline <- ml_load(sc, "iris-fitted/") stream_read_csv(sc, "iris-in") %>% sdf_transform(fitted_pipeline) %>% stream_write_csv("iris-out") ``` **SQL:** SQL transformations can be performed can be performed as follows: ```r stream_read_csv(sc, "iris-in", name = "iris") sdf_sql(sc, "SELECT count(*) FROM iris") %>% stream_write_csv("iris-out") ``` **spark_apply:** `spark_apply()` can also be used by simply piping the stream source: ```r stream_read_csv(sc, "iris-in") %>% spark_apply(I) %>% stream_write_csv("iris-out") ``` `dplyr`, `SQL`, piepeline scoring and `spark_apply()` operations can be combined over the same pipeline: ```r stream_read_csv(sc, "iris-in") %>% select(Sepal_Length, Sepal_Width) %>% sdf_transform(fitted_pipeline) %>% stream_write_csv("iris-out") ``` One can also view the streams by running `view_stream(stream)`: And also support the RStudio Jobs API to view and terminate the stream: Work items: - [x] Initial streaming investigation - [x] Support for reading/writing CSV streams. - [x] Support for reading/writing text, JSON, parquet, Kafka, JDBC and orc streams. - [x] Support for `dplyr` over streams. - [x] Support for `SQL` over streams. - [x] Support for prediction `pipelines` over streams. - [x] Support for `spark_apply()` over streams. - [x] Support for continuous streams. - [x] Support to visualize stream graph. - [x] Support for streams in RStudio Jobs API. - [x] Support for `shiny` over streams. - [x] Fix tests and R CMD checks. - [x] Write tests for streams. Unsupported: - Support for `ml` over structured streams. Fitting over structured streams is unsupported in Spark 2.3, the following resources are tracking progress: - [SPARK-16424](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/SPARK-16424) - [ML Streams Design Doc](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1snh7x7b0dQIlTsJNHLr-IxIFgP43RfRV271YK2qGiFQ/edit) - [ML Streams Prototype](https://github.com/holdenk/spark-structured-streaming-ml)

title: Add `ml_vocabulary()` and `ml_topics_matrix()`
description:
Add `ml_vocabulary()` and `ml_topics_matrix()` to make it easier to interpret LDA output. Closes https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/issues/1353 reported by @alexpavlakis.

```
sc <- spark_connect(master = "local")
fake_data <- data.frame(a = c(1, 2, 3, 4),
                        b = c("the groggy", "frog was", "a very groggy", "frog"))
fake_tbl <- sdf_copy_to(sc, fake_data, overwrite = TRUE)

fake_tokenized <- fake_tbl %>%
  ft_tokenizer(input_col = 'b', output_col = 'tokens')

count_vectorizer_model <- ft_count_vectorizer(sc, input_col = "tokens", output_col = "features",
                    dataset = fake_tokenized)

fake_model <- count_vectorizer_model %>%
  ml_transform(fake_tokenized) %>%
  ml_lda(features_col = 'features', k = 2)

topics_matrix <- ml_topics_matrix(fake_model) 
rownames(topics_matrix) <- ml_vocabulary(count_vectorizer_model)

# > topics_matrix
#             [,1]      [,2]
# frog   0.9248075 0.8520465
# groggy 0.9542146 1.3718052
# was    1.1007057 0.8134825
# a      0.8691240 1.2047227
# the    1.0009945 1.0389219
# very   1.1337509 1.1529417
```

title: Support invoke_static() with package objects
description:
For Scala objects defined as [package objects](http://www.scala-lang.org/docu/files/packageobjects/packageobjects.html), as in:

```scala
package object test {
  def testPackageObject(s : String): String = s
}
```

It was not possible to make use of them in `sparklyr`, now this is supported using:

```r
invoke_static(sc, "sparklyr.test", "testPackageObject", "x")
```

This also unblocks, potentially, access to other fields since we used to only enumerate methods, the code above can be also triggered without syntactic sugar as follows:

```r
invoke(invoke_static(sc, "sparklyr.test.package$", "MODULE$"), "testPackageObject", "x")
```

The motivation of this change is https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/issues/1384 to enable `arrayToArrayList` in [utils](https://github.com/hail-is/hail/blob/449556d7123a6d0978926d70a32e86817dfd2906/src/main/scala/is/hail/utils/package.scala) from the [Hail project](https://hail.is/).

title: Enable Kerberos authentication with Livy
description:
While both Livy and Kerberos are individually supported, using them together is not possible yet.

Currently, `livy_config` considers only Basic authentication. But, if the Livy server is using Kerberos authentication, we need to use "Negotiate (SPNEGO) authentication". If we use curl CLI, `--negotiate` will allow us to use Negotiate. With R/httr, it is available via `httr::authenticate("", "", type = "gssnegotiate")`.

c.f.:
- https://stackoverflow.com/questions/26255964/r-negotiate-authentication-with-rcurl-or-httr
- https://stackoverflow.com/a/38664954

Since it is not as simple as adding one header, it seems better to store it as `sparklyr.livy.auth` config and use it when making a request.

Note that users need to get and cache the ticket priorly, which is described on https://spark.rstudio.com/guides/connections/#kerberos

title: Fix crash during immediate reconnect
description:
`SIGPIPE` exceptions can trigger in R when attempting to write data into a socket that is already closed, reproducing https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/issues/1172 showed that while the active connection is closing, the call to `System.exit(0)` can wait a few ms for the `gatewayServerSocket` to close. When an immediate reconnect is triggered, the reconnect could still reach the previous connection just to see it close when it attempts to write.

The fix is to reduce even more the likelihood of this happening by immediately closing the socket before terminating the process which proved to be much faster than relying on the underlined OS to close this as a side effect of exiting the process.

enable inputting read schema to optimize reads of nested parquet data
description:
Pending https://github.com/apache/spark/pull/16578 spark reads too much data from nested parquet fields. This PR enables users to pass in read schemas (a sub-schema from the full data schema) so that only the nested (and top level) fields of interest are read in. For users with complex nested data this amounts to a huge performance boost.

The `schema` argument can be constructed using the `sparklyr.nested` functions defined here https://mitre.github.io/sparklyr.nested/reference/struct_type.html (which mostly just use the `SQLUtils.getSQLDataType`  from https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/blob/master/inst/livy/spark-1.5.2/sqlutils.scala). 

For example, referencing the schema here https://mitre.github.io/sparklyr.nested/index.html then one could input
```
start_point_schema <- struct_type(sc,
    struct_field(sc, 'altitude', double_type(sc), nullable=FALSE)
)
phases_schema <- struct_type(sc,
  struct_field(sc, 'start_point', start_point_schema, FALSE)
)
data_schema <- struct_type(sc,
  c(struct_field(sc, 'primary_key', string_type(sc), FALSE),
    struct_field(sc, 'phase_sequence', string_type(sc), TRUE),
    struct_field(sc, 'phases', phases_schema, TRUE))
)

df <- spark_read_parquet(sc, ..., schema=data_schema)
```

This would result in not reading any of the `phasts$end_point` data and would read only `phases$start_point$altitude`. With most of the data filtered at read, then doing explode operations (e.g., https://mitre.github.io/sparklyr.nested/reference/sdf_explode.html) is not nearly so expensive.

description:
Adds support for `spark_apply()` under `yarn-cluster` using `spark_apply_bundle()` as a helper function to generate the package bundle.

Sample use for `yarn-cluster`:

```r
dplyr_bundle <- spark_apply_bundle("dplyr")

config <- spark_config()
config$sparklyr.shell.files <- dplyr_bundle
sc <- spark_connect(master = "yarn-cluster", config = config)

iris_tbl <- sdf_copy_to(sc, iris)
spark_apply(iris_tbl, function(df) {
    library(dplyr)
    df %>% select(Sepal_Length)
}, packages = dplyr_bundle)
```

title: Add support under 'yarn-cluster' to wait for available resources
description:
A couple `yarn-cluster` improvements that are blocking usage of this feature under some clusters.

### ACCEPTED State

See https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/issues/1033/ 

Currently, 'yarn-cluster' only supports `sparklyr.yarn.cluster.start.timeout` as a setting to control how long to wait to establish a connection to Yarn and retrieve the running application.

However, for busy clusters, it is currently not possible to wait until the resources become available. 

This information is available under `state` in the Yarn app. Therefore, added support for `sparklyr.yarn.cluster.accepted.timeout` which can be configured to wait for indefinite amounts of time for cluster resources to become available.

### HTTPS Support

See https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/issues/1054/

This PR adds support for HTTPS for `yarn-cluster` which is activated by setting `yarn.http.policy` to `HTTPS_ONLY` in `yarn-site.xml`.

### Other Improvements

Additionally, this PR also adds support to make `yarn-cluster` work without additional `yarn-site.xml` config changes under Amazon EMR.

title: ML improvements
description:
*New Features*

- Adds support for pipelines (#593, #734) and introduce additional functions to support the feature.
- Implements additional Spark ML algorithms
    - Isotonic Regression -- `ml_isotonic_regerssion()`
    - Bisecting K-means -- `ml_bisecting_kmeans()` (#986)
    - Gaussian Mixture -- `ml_gaussian_mixture()`
- Adds support for hyper-parameter tuning via `ml_cross_validator()` and `ml_train_validation_split()`. (#196)
- Improves output of `sdf_predict()` for classification (#762, #605, #928)
- Better support for model persistence by saving/loading pipelines. (https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/issues/1088, #336, #1070, #212)
- Use Spark functions for formula parsing to support formulas with interactions (#554)
- Adds support to separate struct columns in `sdf_separate_column()`.
 (https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/issues/690)
- Adds support for reading libsvm files via `spark_read_libsvm()`.
- `spark_connect()` now defaults to 2.2.0.

*Migration*

- Function and argument names have been changed for consistency with Spark, although old function and variable names are still supported/silently soft-deprecated.
- `ml.options()` is no longer supported.
- ML function signatures
    - `function(tbl, response, features)` is no longer supported, although users can still explicitly pass `response` and `features` arguments.
    - The undocumented(?) `function(formula, data)` signature is no longer supported.
- `ml_tree_feature_importance()` is now `function(model)` instead of `function(sc, model)` since `sc` is redundant, but the previous signature is still supported.
- `ml_save()/ml_load()` no longer attempts to save R metadata. The new `ml_load()` will not be able to load models saved in previous versions.

*TODO before release*

- More informative error messages, i.e. throw errors on the R side instead of showing users Java stack traces, especially for errors around feature and response specification.
- Compatibility with older Spark versions and more informative messages. Currently the tests have been run against 2.1 and 2.2.
- Implement all Spark feature transformers.
- Better test coverage for some ML algorithms.
- Consider adding `summary()` methods to ML model objectsl
- Consider exposing developer API to for extending `sparklyr` to work with customer transformers and estimators.
- Drop support for Spark 1.5.x

Issue tracking pipelines work: https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/issues/944

title: Enable `yarn-cluster` in CDH clusters
description:
Enable `yarn-cluster` in CDH clusters, say running:

```r
library(sparklyr)

Sys.setenv(JAVA_HOME="/usr/lib/jvm/java-7-oracle-cloudera/")
Sys.setenv(SPARK_HOME = '/opt/cloudera/parcels/CDH/lib/spark')
Sys.setenv(YARN_CONF_DIR = '/opt/cloudera/parcels/CDH/lib/spark/conf/yarn-conf')

conf <- spark_config()

sc <- spark_connect(master = "yarn-cluster", 
                    config = conf,
                    version = "1.6.0")
```

The main fix here was to query the YARN API to retrieve the given container host; seems `yarn-cluster` is not required to run on the driver node in all cases and therefore, can't be assumed to run on a particular node with `config$sparklyr.gateway.address`.

References:
- [ResourceManager REST API’s.](https://hadoop.apache.org/docs/stable/hadoop-yarn/hadoop-yarn-site/ResourceManagerRest.html#Cluster_Applications_API)
- [Deployment Modes](https://www.cloudera.com/documentation/enterprise/5-4-x/topics/cdh_ig_running_spark_on_yarn.html#concept_asc_2hr_gs)

title: Fix slow printing of spark dataframes
description:
See https://github.com/tidyverse/tibble/issues/285.

Bottom line, `print.tbl_spark` is too slow since `dbplyr` started using `tibble` as the default way of printing records, but `tibble::truncate` uses `nrow()` which uses `dim` which resolves to `dim.tbl_spark` and cause a full run over the dataset.

I explored a few alternative solutions:
1. Implement `print.tbl_spark`: Not great since a lot of functionality is implemented as private methods in `dbplyr` so we would have to copy all that or remove funcitonality like printing `order-bys`.
2. Workaround in `tibble`, hard to coordinate this since this is high-pri for `sparklyr`.

Users that make use of `dim`, `nrow` and `ncol` would have to use `sdf_dim`, `sdf_nrow` and `sdf_ncol` instead.

Fix `invoke()` for integer arrays containing NAs
description:
See https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/issues/971

Eventhough found through `spark_apply()`, I was able to reproduce this issue for `invoke()` calls as follows:

```scala
class TestClass() {
  private var result: Array[Row] = Array[Row]()

  def setResultArraySeq(resultParam: Array[Any]) = {
    result = resultParam.map(x => Row.fromSeq(x.asInstanceOf[Array[_]].toSeq))
  }
}
```

```r
all_results <- structure(list(B = c(NA, 1L, NA, 1L, 1L, NA)), 
                          .Names = c("B"), 
                          row.names = c(NA,-6L), 
                          class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

all_data <- lapply(1:nrow(all_results), function(i) as.list(all_results[i,]))

tc <- invoke_new(sc, "sparklyr.TestClass")
invoke(tc, "setResultArraySeq", all_data[1])    
```

```
Error: java.io.EOFException
	at java.io.DataInputStream.readInt(DataInputStream.java:392)
	at sparklyr.Serializer$.readInt(serializer.scala:82)
	at sparklyr.Serializer$$anonfun$readIntArr$1.apply(serializer.scala:126)
	at sparklyr.Serializer$$anonfun$readIntArr$1.apply(serializer.scala:126)
	at scala.collection.TraversableLike$$anonfun$map$1.apply(TraversableLike.scala:234)
	at scala.collection.TraversableLike$$anonfun$map$1.apply(TraversableLike.scala:234)
	at scala.collection.immutable.Range.foreach(Range.scala:160)
```

The problem is similar to https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/issues/774 where we try to encode lists as `Array[]` but only if there are not `NA`s present since Scala does not support them in all data types, the fix was applied to `character`s but `integer` types also fall into this category.

The issue was that since an `NA` was detected while serializing a `integer` array, the serializer would only write the `serdeType` for the `NA` but not a value, which made the contract corrupt for the Scala `deserializer` which assumes one can read an integer array in a single pass.

title: `ml_lda` improvements towards supporting full text classification
description:
See https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/issues/471.

Followed a couple `LDA` references like [Spark's Latent Dirichlet allocation (LDA)](https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/mllib-clustering.html#latent-dirichlet-allocation-lda), [this](https://gist.github.com/jkbradley/ab8ae22a8282b2c8ce33) and [this](https://dzone.com/articles/spark-lda-a-complete-example-of-clustering-algorit). We were missing a couple features like:

1. Ability to remove stop words.
2. Ability to describe the topics.
3. Ability to adjust max iterations which happen to be relevant for `LDA`.
4. Ability to choose the optimuzer between `online` and `em`.

Which are now implemented with this PR.

## Sample Run

Here is what I tried, first some initialization:

```r
install.packages("tidytext")
install.packages("janeaustenr")
install.packages("stringr")

library(tidytext)
library(stringr)
library(dplyr)

original_books <- austen_books() %>%
  group_by(book) %>%
  mutate(linenumber = row_number(),
         chapter = cumsum(str_detect(text, regex("^chapter [\\divxlc]",
                                                 ignore_case = TRUE)))) %>%
  ungroup()

paragraphs <- original_books %>%
  unnest_tokens("paragraph", text, token = "paragraphs")

sc <- spark_connect(master = "local[4]")
```
## janeaustenr dataset

Using `janeaustenr` we get the following,

```r
paragraphs_tbl <- copy_to(sc, paragraphs, overwrite = TRUE)

paragraphs_tokens <- paragraphs_tbl %>%
  ft_regex_tokenizer("paragraph", "tokens", "[ 0-9\\.,!?\\(\\)\\\":\\-]+") %>%
  ft_stop_words_remover("tokens", "better_tokens")

paragraphs_lda <- paragraphs_tokens %>%
  ft_count_vectorizer("better_tokens", "features") %>%
  ml_lda("features", k = 4)

title: enhancements for ml_random_forest()
description:
This PR adds the following tuning arguments to `ml_random_forest()`:

- `col.sample.rate`: Column sampling rate at each split (*not* per tree.) Spark ML calls this `featureSubsetStrategy` and requires a *string* input, e.g. "onethird", "sqrt", or "n", with `"when n is in the range (0, 1.0], use n * number of features. When n is in the range (1, number of features), use n features"`... which I think is really confusing. In this PR I'm requiring a *double* between 0 and 1. `NULL` defaults to the Spark ML `auto` strategy which equates to `sqrt(k)/k` for classification and `1/3` for regression, where `k` is number of features.

- `impurity`: The measure for info gain calculation at each split. Spark ML supports one of "gini" and "entropy" for classification (defaults to gini) and "variance" for regression. Input validation is included in our implementation.

- `min.info.gain`: Info gain required to split. This is an absolute number and not relative improvement.

- `min.rows`: Minimum number of observations each node must have after split. Spark ML calls this `minInstancesPerNode`, h2o calls this `min_rows` and R randomForest calls it `nodesize`. I like h2o's choice here.

- `thresholds`: This is used in multiclass classification to introduce bias to the predictions. Basically users can pass a vector of numbers (t_1, t_2, ..., t_K) where K is the number of classes, and the probabilities will be adjusted to be (p_1/t_1, p_2/t_2, ..., p_K/t_K), where the p_i's are the raw probabilities. The predicted label would be the one with highest adjusted probability.

- `seed`: Used for column and row sampling.

First time copy of all packages using `spark_apply` goes for about:

```r

   user  system elapsed 
  0.288   0.804  10.097

```r
system.time(iris_tbl %>% spark_apply(function(e) system.file("samples/sample.warc", package = "sparkwarc"), packages = TRUE))
   user  system elapsed 
  0.048   0.000   2.660

This is not ideal since without packages we get:

   user  system elapsed 
  0.036   0.000   0.774

title: Add support for Yarn Cluster
description:
@statmatt willing to try this PR attempting to add `YARN-CLUSTER` support?

**Background:**
- *Yarn-Client* runs the `sparklyr` backend on the same machine. In the past, just like `sparkR`, `sparklyr` used a file to communicate the port number back to the client. This restriction was removed with the [Gateway PR](https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/pull/238).
- *Yarn-Cluster* runs the `sparklyr` backend potentially on a different machine, the remote driver. While this would be challenging to accomplish with the ports file, using the `sparklyr.gateway.address` config option should be enough to workaround this.

**Implementation:**
In order to support `YARN-CLIENT`, it is my understanding that all we need to do is get this information from `yarn-site.xml` which should be set under `YARN_CONF_DIR`, that's about it.

**Example:**
This PR needs additional testing but worth trying out as follows:

```r
devtools::install_github("rstudio/sparklyr", ref = "feature/yarn-cluster")
```

```r
sc <- spark_connect(master = "yarn-cluster")
```

or explicitly as:

```r
sc <- spark_connect(
  master = "yarn-cluster",
  config = list(sparklyr.gateway.address = "<driver-node>")
)
```

title: Terminate connection under no status errors.
description:
This PR fixes crashes similar to https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/issues/785.

At times, one can get a `"No status is returned. The sparklyr backend might have failed."` error. This means that the `sparklyr` backend experienced such a critical error that a status was not returned (in scala, `exceptions` are recoverable while [error](http://docs.oracle.com/javase/1.5.0/docs/api/java/lang/Error.html) should not).  For instances, at times Spark might throw an [OutOfMemoryError](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/7/docs/api/java/lang/OutOfMemoryError.html) (as in https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/issues/783).

The fix is to terminate the connection when no status is returned, if an exception is thrown, the `sparklyr` backend will catch it and serialize it; however, errors are not (and should not) so we terminate the entire connection since the backend is effectively in a bad state.

Finally, we shouldn't be using `assert` for recoverable exceptions, this change replaces `assert` with `IllegalArgumentException`.

title: Avoid crashing r-session while invoking array character with NAs #780
description:
The following crashes the r-session after executing a couple times the `invoke_static`, more info under https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/issues/780:

```r
library(sparklyr)
sc <- spark_connect(master = "local", version = "2.1.0")

naChar <- NA
class(naChar) <- "character"

invoke_static(
    sc,
    "sparklyr.Utils",
    "classExists",
    list(list(naChar), list("a")))
```

The problem here is that the function parameters with arrays of `character` types containing `NAs`, get serialized as an array of `characters` (correct) but when the `NA` gets serialized serialized to `void()` and nothing gets written in the binary buffer. This is fine while writing single `NA` in `character`s since the null type precedes, in case of arrays all have the same type. Since NAs are not supported in Scala character arrays.

On the scala side, since nothing is serialized for `NA`, the length of the character string is read afterward and allocates memory. In this case, it is too much memory that crashes the Scala backend with an OutOfMemory exception, which prevents the backend to writing the result back into the socket, which crashes the r-session when trying to read a value that is not in the socket buffer. This last part seems like a bug to me in R, taking a look at this as well since I think there are more ways to crash R following this pattern even if we fix this code path.

title: Make compute cache data inmemory by default to fix #721
description:
From investigating https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/issues/721... We currently,

```r
library(sparklyr)
library(dplyr)
sc <- spark_connect(master = "local", version = "2.1.0")
iris_tbl <- copy_to(sc, iris)

iris_tbl %>% compute()
```

`compute()` creates a named temporary table for the given query. While this could be useful in some cases, say:

```r
iris_tbl %>% select(Species) %>% compute(name = "iris_species")
tbl(sc, "iris_species")
```

However, there is also an explicit assumption that `compute()`, from dplyr's help:
> compute() stores results in a remote temporary table.

This  was the assumption at least on https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/issues/721.

In retrospect, `compute()` is not very interesting as it is implemented today in `sparklyr` since it doesn't take advantage of Spark functions and does not "store results in a remote temporary table".

The proposed change is to cache into memory the result of `compute()` which is a more natural operation from `dplyr` while using `sparklyr`.

title: Fix spark_connect(master = "local") when version isn't set
description:
This PR fixes an issue introduced by 84e7ce09a1769440bb92bb7196c08db18c943158 where connection in local mode fails when `version` isn't specified.

Current behavior:

```
> sc <- spark_connect(master = "local")
Error in shell_connection(master = master, spark_home = spark_home, app_name = app_name,  : 
                            Failed to connect to Spark (SPARK_HOME is not set). 
```

With patch:

```
> sc <- spark_connect(master = "local")
* Using Spark: 2.0.0
```

title: hive operators for regex matching
description:
This change adds `%like%`, `%rlike%`, and `%regexp%` which correspond to `LIKE`, `RLIKE`, and `REGEXP`, respectively, from https://cwiki.apache.org/confluence/display/Hive/LanguageManual+UDF for regex matching.

Closes #761, closes #329

title: Validate hostname is correct while creating spark context to fix #532
description: This PR addresses a configuration issue in Spark <= 2.0.1, while not a problem in `sparklyr`, several `sparklyr` users have reported this problem. For instance, using EC2+R+Conda+sparklyr triggers this problem: The logs show that `tachyon.hadoop.TFS` could not be initialized: ``` Caused by: java.lang.NoClassDefFoundError: Could not initialize class tachyon.hadoop.TFS at sun.reflect.NativeConstructorAccessorImpl.newInstance0(Native Method) at sun.reflect.NativeConstructorAccessorImpl.newInstance(NativeConstructorAccessorImpl.java:57) at sun.reflect.DelegatingConstructorAccessorImpl.newInstance(DelegatingConstructorAccessorImpl.java:45) at java.lang.reflect.Constructor.newInstance(Constructor.java:526) at java.lang.Class.newInstance(Class.java:383) at java.util.ServiceLoader$LazyIterator.next(ServiceLoader.java:373) ... 72 more ”Warning message in create_hive_context_v1(sc): ``` However, one can configure `sparklyr` with: ``` spark_install(version = "1.6.2, logging = "TRACE") ``` which will increase logging, and `spark_log(sc)` will show a full stack trace that looks more like: ``` Error: java.net.UnknownHostException: ip-172-30-0-220: ip-172-30-0-220: Name or service not known at java.net.InetAddress.getLocalHost(InetAddress.java:1496) at sun.reflect.NativeMethodAccessorImpl.invoke0(Native Method) at sun.reflect.NativeMethodAccessorImpl.invoke(NativeMethodAccessorImpl.java:57) at sun.reflect.DelegatingMethodAccessorImpl.invoke(DelegatingMethodAccessorImpl.java:43) at java.lang.reflect.Method.invoke(Method.java:606) at sparklyr.Invoke$.invoke(invoke.scala:94) at sparklyr.StreamHandler$.handleMethodCall(stream.scala:89) at sparklyr.StreamHandler$.read(stream.scala:55) at sparklyr.BackendHandler.channelRead0(handler.scala:49) at sparklyr.BackendHandler.channelRead0(handler.scala:14) ``` This problem even triggers while running `spark-shell`. However, given that so many users have reported this, is worth to at least warn about by checking this ourselves. The change introduces a call to `java.net.InetAddress.getLocalHost` which is also used by Spark, Hadoop, and many others pieces of the stack which will fail under this configurations. The fix is usually to get the hostname say, by running `hostname` and then adding this entry in the `/etc/hosts` file.

title: Serialize NaN in long columns as doubles
description:

title: Format NEWS for 0.6 Release
description:
Formats the NEWS file grouping changes by feature area:

# Sparklyr 0.6.0 (UNRELEASED)

### Distributed R

- Added `spark_apply()` to run distributed r code at scale.

### External Data

- Added `spark_read_source()`. This function reads data from a
  Spark data source which can be loaded through an Spark package.

- Added support for `mode = "overwrite"` and `mode = "append"` to
  `spark_write_csv`.

- `spark_write_table` now supports saving to default Hive path.

- Improved performance of `spark_read_csv` reading remote data when
  `infer_schema = FALSE`.

- Added `spark_read_jdbc`. This function reads from a JDBC connection
  into a Spark DataFrame.

- Renamed `spark_load_table` and `spark_save_table` into `spark_read_table`
  and `spark_write_table` for consistency with existing `spark_read_*` and
  `spark_write_*` functions.

- Added support to specify a vector of column names in `spark_read_csv` to
  specify column names without having to set the type of each column.

- Improved `copy_to`, `sdf_copy_to` and `dbWriteTable` performance under
  `yarn-client` mode.

### dplyr

- Support for `dplyr 0.6` which among many improvements, increases
  performance in some queries by making use of a new query optimizer.

- `sample_frac` takes a fraction instead of a percent to match `dplyr`.

- Improved support in dplyr commands to handle multiple databases.

- Improved performance of `sample_n()` and `sample_frac()` by using TABLESAMPLE
  query.
  
### Databases

- Added `src_databases`. This function list all the available databases.

- Added `tbl_change_db()`. This function changes current database.

### DataFrames

- Added `sdf_len`, `sdf_seq` and `sdf_along` to help generate numeric
  sequences as Spark DataFrames.

- Added `spark_set_checkpoint_dir()`, `spark_get_checkpoint_dir()`, and 
  `sdf_checkpoint()` to enable checkpointing.
  
- Added `sdf_broadcast()` which can be used to hint the query
  optimizer to perform a broadcast join in cases where a shuffle
  hash join is planned but not optimal.

- Added `sdf_repartition()` and `sdf_num_partitions()` to support
  repartitioning and getting the number of partitions of Spark DataFrames.

- Added `sdf_bind_rows()` and `sdf_bind_cols()` -- these functions
  are the `sparklyr` equivalent of `dplyr::bind_rows()` and 
  `dplyr::bind_cols()`.
  
- Added `sdf_separate_column()` -- this function allows one to separate
  components of an array / vector column into separate scalar-valued
  columns.

- `sdf_with_sequential_id()` now supports `from` parameter to choose the
  starting value of the id column.

- Added `sdf_pivot()`. This function provides a mechanism for constructing
  pivot tables, using Spark's 'groupBy' + 'pivot' functionality, with a
  formula interface similar to that of `reshape2::dcast()`.
  
### MLlib

- Implemented `residuals()` and `sdf_residuals()` for Spark linear 
  regression and GLM models. The former returns a R vector while 
  the latter returns a `tbl_spark` of training data with a `residuals`
  column added.
  
- Added `ml_model_data()`, used for extracting data associated with
  Spark ML models.

- The `ml_save()` and `ml_load()` functions gain a `meta`
  argument, allowing users to specify where R-level model
  metadata should be saved independently of the Spark model
  itself. This should help facilitate the saving and loading
  of Spark models used in non-local connection scenarios.

- `ml_als_factorization` now supports the implicit matrix factorization
   and nonnegative least square options.

- Added `ft_count_vectorizer()`. This function can be used to transform
  columns of a Spark DataFrame so that they might be used as input to `ml_lda()`.
  This should make it easier to invoke `ml_lda()` on Spark data sets.
  
### Broom
  
- Implemented `tidy`, `augment`, and `glance` from tidyverse/broom for
  `ml_model_generalized_linear_regression` and `ml_model_linear_regression`
  models.
  
### R Compatibility

- Implemented `cbind.tbl_spark()`. This method works by first generating
  index columns using `sdf_with_sequential_id()` then performing `inner_join()`.
  Note that dplyr `_join()` functions should still be used for DataFrames 
  with common keys since they are less expensive.

### Connections

- Added `sparklyr.log.console` to redirect logs to console, useful
  to troubleshooting `spark_connect`.

- Added `sparklyr.backend.args` as config option to enable passing
  parameters to the `sparklyr` backend.

- Improved logging while establishing connections to `sparklyr`.

- Improved `spark_connect` performance.

- Implemented new configuration checks to proactively report connection errors
  in Windows.

- While connecting to spark from Windows, setting the `sparklyr.verbose` option
  to `TRUE` prints detailed configuration steps.
  
### Compilation

- Added support for `jar_dep` in the compilation specification to
  support additional `jars` through `spark_compile`.

- `spark_compile` now prints deprecation warnings.

- Added `download_scalac()` to assist downloading all the Scala compilers
  required to build using `compile_package_jars` and provided support for
  using any `scalac` minor versions while looking for the right compiler.

### Backend

- Improved backend logging by adding type and session id prefix.

### Miscellaneous

- Implemented `type_sum.jobj` (from tibble) to enable better printing of jobj
  embedded in data frames.

- Added `spark_home_set` to set with ease `SPARK_HOME`, specially
  useful while teaching the basics of Spark and `sparklyr.

- Added support for the `sparklyr.ui.connections` option, which adds additional
  connection options into the new connections dialog. The
  `rstudio.spark.connections` option is now deprecated.

- Implemented the "new connection dialog" as a Shiny application to be able to
  support newer versions of RStudio that deprecate current connections ui.

### Bug Fixes
  
- Fixed backend issue that affects systems where `localhost` does
  not resolve properly to the loopback address.

- Fixed issue collecting data frames containing `\n`.

- Spark Null objects (objects of class NullType) discovered within numeric
  vectors are now collected as NAs, rather than lists of NAs.

- Fixed warning while connecting with livy and improved 401 message.

- Fixed issue in `spark_read_parquet()` and other read methods in which
  `spark_normalize_path()` would not work in some platforms while loading
  data using custom protocols like s3n:// for Amazon S3.

- Resolved issue in `spark_save()` / `load_table()` to support saving / loading
  data and added path parameter in `spark_load_table()` for consistency with
  other functions.

title: Implement Livy connections
description:
This PR implements `livy` connections in `sparklyr` by starting and making use of an interactive Scala Livy session. The basic use of `livy` in `sparklyr` is as follows:

```{r}
library(sparklyr)
livy_install()
livy_service_start()

sc <- spark_connect(master = "local", method = "livy")
copy_to(sc, iris)
src_tbls(sc)

spark_disconnect(sc)
livy_service_stop()
```

**Background**: Livy supports Scala, Python and R sessions; with the R sessions being served by an `sparkR` client (https://github.com/cloudera/livy#session-kind). We could, potentially, send a PR to use `sparklyr` as a type of session to Livy; however, we would still have to write an `sparklyr` client to serialize into the remote Livy `sparklyr` session running in Livy which adds additional complexity compared to using `sparklyr` as a client to an Scala interactive session and therefore, this approach was taken.

**Design**: This implementation reuses most of the `sparklyr` backend in Livy. The motivation behind reusing most of the backend code is that, otherwise:
 1. Would require to re-implement method signature-matching that the `sparklyr` backend supports. For instance, `invoke(jobj, list("a"))` or `invoke(jobj, c("a"))` is mapped to an scala type with the correct conversion; there are other more complicated mappings involving maps and other structures.
 2. Would require to re-implement serialization to match the `sparklyr` backend. For instance, fetching an Scala nested array `Array[Array[], Array[]]` correctly into a `list(list(), list())` requires custom serialization.

The `sparklyr` backend is reused by pre-processing the `scala` sources into livy-compatible sources that are compiled using `livy_sources_refresh()` and placed for distribution under `inst/livy/*.scala`. When a livy session starts, those files are sourced into the livy session. Once the `sparklyr` backend is loaded, instead of using a socket to serialize binary data to the backend, serialization is performed in`sparklyr` by executing `livy` commands in base64, for instance, `sparklyr` would send the following `livy` statement to initialize the connections:

```{scala}
var sparklyrRetVar_0 = LivyUtils.invokeFromBase64("AAAAHm9yZy5hcGFjaGUuc3BhcmsuU3BhcmtDb250ZXh0AAAAAAEAAAAMZ2V0T3JDcmVhdGUAAAAAAA=="
```

In the remote Scala session through `livy`, `LivyUtils.invokeFromBase64` would deserialize this call and map it to the `sparklyr` backend, get the binary response and encode it back as base64 to which livy returns a `text/plain` response of:

```
sparklyrRetVar_0: String = AAAAAGoAAAABMA==
```

This response is now parsed in the `sparklyr` client and the base64 decoded back to a binary response. In cases where the response is too big and gets truncated, a livy magic is used to return this as json, for instance, by executing the following `livy` statement:

```
%json sparklyrRetVar_0
```

Once the serialization is in place, the rest of `sparklyr` works as expected and no fixes had to be performed in higher layers of `sparklyr`, say: `dplyr`, `ml` nor `extensions`.

**Known Issues**:
  1. Serialization of large datasets through `copy_to` is currently failing in Livy, investigation to mitigate this underway.

title: Backend improvements to support context and unregister
description:
1. Currently, the backend can register itself into an existing `sparklyr` gateway, but does not clean up the registration when the backend session terminates. This is not a problem so far since session-ids are never reused; however, for extensions like `sparkworker` that use the backend while generating RDDs, the RDDs can be recomputed at any time and the session-id reused, which causes hangs, etc. Regardless of `sparkworker`, it's a good practice to unregister sessions to prevent collisions in long-lived backends.

2. To improve extensibility, the backend now supports a custom `hostContext` string which can be used arbitrarily by classes using the backend. For `sparkworker`, this is used to track the RDD class and map the results back from the `RScript`.

3. Make use of thread-safe map, not really an issue unless multiple backends are instantiated in the same machine which is easy to hit under `sparkworker` on local mode using data with multiple partitions. Additionally, need to increase number of default threads to 10, since there is overlap while handling multiple clients (this setting is configurable but even simple scenarios in distributed execution hit this issue)

title: Implement broom for ML glm and linear regression models
description:
This PR adds implementations of `tidy`, `augment`, and `glance` for ML GLM and linear regression models (no logistic regression yet.)

Design decisions:

- @kevinushey We discussed whether to include a `style` argument so users could choose between `dot.case` or something else for column names since some versions of Spark don't support `.` in column names. I realized this wasn't necessary because the only methods this would affect are `tidy` and `glance`, whose outputs are always small `data.frame`. `broom` chose to prefix names of added columns in `augment` with dots, but we can't have column names starting with dots in Spark anyway. In my `augment` output, the added columns are simply named `fitted` and `resid`.

- The `type.residuals` argument to `augment` defaults to `"working"`, i.e. `actual - predicted` or prediction error. For GLM, this is different from the default for `residuals()` and `sdf_residuals()`, which is `"deviance"` (to be consistent with base R methods.) This default is chosen because 1) we don't support anything other than "working" when `newdata` is supplied, so it would avoid confusion, also 2) IMO most people think prediction error when they see "residuals" in the ML context.

- Working residual is defined to be `actual - predicted` instead of `predicted - actual`; just agreeing with base R and MLlib here.

Related: https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/issues/670, https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/issues/557

title: Support a login prefixes in backend service
description:
This PR standardizes prefixes in the server logs since:
1. The backend can currently run in `gateway` or `backend` mode when is not acting as a gateway but it was not straightforward to spot which mode the backend was running in from the logs.
2. Most backend log entries print the `sessionId` themselves, but this is information that should be tracked across each log instance to effectively diagnose problems.
3. To support distributed computation, we would need a new backend mode `worker` which makes logs even harder to read.

This PR improves logging as follows for a simple connection:

```
library(sparklyr)
sc <- spark_connect(master = "local", version = "2.1.0")
spark_log(sc, filter = "sparklyr:")
```

```
17/05/22 23:01:10 INFO sparklyr: Session (1722) is starting under 172.16.158.1/127.0.0.1 port 8880
17/05/22 23:01:10 INFO sparklyr: Session (1722) found port 8880 is available
17/05/22 23:01:10 INFO sparklyr: Gateway (1722) is waiting for sparklyr client to connect to port 8880
17/05/22 23:01:10 INFO sparklyr: Gateway (1722) accepted connection

title: residuals() and sdf_residuals() for lm/glm
description:
This PR implements `residuals()` and `sdf_residual()` methods for Spark ML linear regression and GLM regression models. The former returns a R vector and the latter returns a `tbl_spark`.

After looking at the MLlib code I discovered that it wasn't possible to simply "select" a residuals column *in addition* to the modeling DataFrame. The methods to calculate the ingredients for residuals (e.g. deviance) were not exposed in the API so we can't invoke them directly (or via reflection.) Instead of implementing a family/distribution hierarchy in sparklyr, I'm proposing that we "cbind" the output that's provided by the Spark API (i.e. a DataFrame with one column) with the the modeling dataset. Since the residuals output from Spark and the training dataset have the same distribution/order in the cluster (it's just a udf map), we can invoke `rdd.zip` which doesn't involve shuffling. This mechanism is implemented in the unexported function `sdf_fast_bind_cols()`.

The naming of the output column `"residuals"` was chosen to be consistent with `"predictions"` in `sdf_predict()`.

Related: https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/issues/670, https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/issues/557

Previous PR: https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/pull/672

title: Implement sdf_bind_rows and sdf_bind_cols
description:
**Ready for review**

This PR would add `sdf_bind_rows` and `sdf_bind_cols` which mirror `dplyr::bind_rows` and `dplyr::bind_cols`.

I need some help with the `sdf_bind_cols` implementation: the issue relates to our calling `substitute()` in `cbind.tbl_spark()` in order to generate an informative message when there's a mismatch in number of rows (https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/blob/dad79603b3b9779930283411061c85be7e93aeac/R/mutation.R#L56-L68)

The behavior in this commit:

```
df1a <- data_frame(a = 1:3, b = letters[1:3])
df3a <- data_frame(e = 1:2, f = letters[1:2])

sc <- spark_connect(master = "local")
df1a_tbl <- copy_to(sc, df1a)
df3a_tbl <- copy_to(sc, df3a)

cbind(df1a_tbl, df3a_tbl)
# Error in cbind(deparse.level, ...) : 
#   Not all inputs have the same number of rows, for example:
#   tbl nrow
# 1 df3a_tbl    2
# 2 df1a_tbl    3 

sdf_bind_cols(df1a_tbl, df3a_tbl)
# Error in cbind(deparse.level, ...) : 
#   Not all inputs have the same number of rows, for example:
#   tbl nrow
# 1   2    2
# 2   1    3 
```

To make this work, we'd need to ship the expressions passed to `sdf_bind_cols()` through the call to `cbind()`. This is made more complicated since we need to support lists of `tbl_spark`. There should be some `rlang` tricks available to make this work, but I can't wrap my head around it.

Any comments appreciated with this or other parts of the PR.

title: Implement spark_read_source
description:
See: https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/issues/608

This adds basic support for reading external sources, as in:

Install Cassandra:

```
curl -OL http://downloads.datastax.com/community/dsc.tar.gz
tar -xzf dsc.tar.gz 
cd dsc-cassandra-3.0.9/bin
./cassandra
```

Create table:

```
cd dsc-cassandra-3.0.9/bin
./cqlsh
CREATE KEYSPACE dev WITH REPLICATION = {
   'class':'SimpleStrategy','replication_factor':1};
USE dev;
CREATE TABLE emp (empid int primary key, emp_name varchar);
INSERT INTO emp (empid, emp_name) VALUES (1, 'Fred Smith');
```

From `sparklyr`:

```{r}
library(sparklyr)

config <- spark_config()
config[["sparklyr.defaultPackages"]] <- c(
   "datastax:spark-cassandra-connector:2.0.0-RC1-s_2.11")

sc <- spark_connect(master = "local",
                    version = "2.1.0",
                    config = config)

spark_read_source(
  sc,
  "emp",
  "org.apache.spark.sql.cassandra",
  list(
    keyspace = "dev",
    table = "emp"))
```

```
Source:     table<emp> [?? x 2]
Database:   spark_connection

  empid   emp_name
  <int>      <chr>
1     1 Fred Smith
```

Make sure to match the Cassandra connection version with the Spark version, the full list is available here: https://spark-packages.org/package/datastax/spark-cassandra-connector

See also https://github.com/AkhilNairAmey/crassy and extension being developed to read data from Cassandra with ease.

title: Icons for Spark and Livy connections
Supporting sparklyr in Databricks clusters
description:
## What changes are proposed in this pull request?
This patch adds support for Databricks Spark clusters by adding a method type to `spark_connect`. When `method = 'databricks'`, there is no need for any additional arguments to `spark_connect`.

## Implementation details
The new internal `databricks_connection()` function, does two main things:
1. Makes an internal Databricks call to start the sparklyr backend on the currently attached cluster. This call passes the current location of sparklyr JARs to Databricks backend. The backend will perform the work on searching and find the right JAR and will call its main method.
2. Uses the gateway port returned from step 1 to establish gateway and backend connections

We think sparklyr is going to be an active project with multiple releases in coming months. As a result, we think hard coding the JARs in Databricks spark images will tie users to older versions of the project. We will continue using the JARs that are installed by the R package.

In Databricks notebooks and jobs, the JVM and Spark Context are managed by Databricks. Therefore, applications need to use the existing context and using `spark-submit` will not work. Also, in Databricks notebooks SparkR connection is already established and provides a mechanism for calling into the JVM. We are using SparkR to bootstrap the sparklyr connection

title: Improve copy_to perf under yarn-client
description:
Using `sparklyr 0.5` from CRAN and a 1 master / 1 worker EMR cluster:

```
> library(sparklyr)
> sc <- spark_connect(master = "yarn-client")
> library(nycflights13)
> system.time(flights_tbl <- copy_to(sc, flights, overwrite = TRUE))
   user  system elapsed 
 22.344   0.820  49.741 
```

This change enables using the save-csv and load-csv approach we already support in local installs in yarn-client.

When `spark_read_csv` is used, it assumes files are accessible from worker nodes, this allows local installs to read files fast but it' not supported in clusters since the files are not distributed to the worker nodes by default.

To overcome this limitation, this fix uses the scala csv reader in `yarn-client`, which does not run in the worker nodes, but rather in the master machine (at least for `yarn-client`). This fix can be potentially extended; however, this might not work in all cluster configurations, for instance, this wouldn't work in `yarn-cluster` and have not tested mesos, etc.

Results:

```
> devtools::install_github("rstudio/sparklyr", ref = "feature/copy-perf-yarn-client")

> library(sparklyr)
> sc <- spark_connect(master = "yarn-client")
> library(nycflights13)
> system.time(flights_tbl <- copy_to(sc, flights, overwrite = TRUE))
   user  system elapsed 
 11.428   0.376  25.701 
```

This can improve by 2-4 seconds by using the `repartition` parameter as in: `copy_to(sc, flights, overwrite = TRUE, repartition = 8)` not much of a gain for the `flights` dataset but might be interesting for other datasets.

See also: https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/issues/487

title: Fix Livy for Spark 2.0
description:
Livy 0.3.0 with Spark 2.0 does not support the use of magic referencing a variable executed in the previous statement, which we use to retrieve data as `json` when the response is too long. This change makes `%json <var name>` the default while retrieving any object through Livy.

It also moves the permissions checks from `spark_connect.livy_connection` to `livy_install` which is more appropriate since some systems, like EMR, should not be modified on connection.

title: Implement dynamic hadoop selection in shiny app
description:
This PR implements dynamic hadoop selection in the sparklyr connections shiny app.

There is a bit of complexity since:

 1. **sparkVersion -> hadoopVersion**: Meaning that the spark version listbox changes the hadoop version listbox
 2. **(sparkVersion, hadoopVersion) -> triggerInstallPrompt**: Both listboxes trigger a message box to require installation of spark.
 3.  **triggerInstallPrompt -> updateCode**: Triggering the install prompt also affects the generate code.

To solve this:

 1. **sparkVersion -> (sparkCurrentVersion, triggerInstallPrompt, invalidateCode)**: The spark listbox changes a `sparkCurrentVersion` global variable (to track state), recreates the hadoopVersion listbox, check for install prompt and invalidates code if needed. This solves the case where the spark listbox changes.
 2. **hadoopVersion -> (triggersInstallPrompt, invalidateCode)**: Only when the hadoop listboxchanges, we manually check install prompt and invalidate code if needed
 3. **invalidateCode -> updateCode**: When code invalidated, we update code.
 4. **avoid updates while initializing**: We track state to not trigger any prompts while initializing the app.

@jcheng5: This PR is not as elegant as I would want it to be; therefore, would love to hear suggestion on how to make this interaction cleaner in shiny apps.

title: added waiting state
description:
To fix the issue addressed at https://github.com/rstudio/sparklyr/issues/383, added waiting state to livy connection. As far as I understand, livy's waiting state just means that the statement is waiting for server to execute, as you can see from here: https://github.com/cloudera/livy/commit/b4642b193956b287bb1c1b32bafe4c5a15e71eac

So I thought it would make sense to wait for the waiting status too, since that will eventually transition into running and get finished. Not sure about writing test cases, but after I fixed this, I could make livy work in my cluster. Any feedback will be appreciated.

This change implements the SparklyR end of the new RStudio connection contract. Major changes:

- Functions performing actions now generally perform them directly (formerly they sent the code to the IDE, where it was evaluated directly; we can always change this later by having the package use the rstudioapi to emit code to the console)

title: Refactor copy_to into sdf_import
description:
This is a merge from the functionality in `copy_to` (the copying based on serialization methods to support cluster copies) and the functionality in `sdf_import` (the hashing and conversion to data frame if needed).

Two reasons fopr this change:
1) Is confusing to users that only `copy_to` is redocumented in the `dplyr` documentation. Instead, we want `sdf_copy_to` to be the default entry point for documentation since there are users that use `sparklyr` but not `dplyr`.
2) `sdf_import` does not support copying into a cluster where the HDFS file that is persisted is not available to all nodes, therefore, we use the `string_serializer` as needed in `sdf_import` as well.

I'm also planning to remove `copy_to` from the documentation and rename the "dplyr Interface" section into "dplyr Extensions" since we want to not re-document each dplyr function.

CC: @kevinushey
